news.title: Ashley Hinson's Race vs. Josh Turek Tightens as Trump Plans Iowa Rallies
news.text: A new Marist poll that released on Thursday shows that Republican Ashley Hinson is gaining on Democrat Josh Turek in the race for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat as President Donald Trump plans to visit the Hawkeye State next week. Iowa is among this year's most competitive Senate races, as Turek and Hinson vie for the open seat left by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Polls continue to show a tight race between the two candidates after their first debate last week, where tariffs, immigration and voting records played a major role. A second debate was held on Tuesday night, where again the candidates sparred over Iran, tariffs and immigration. The poll offers new insight into the close race only weeks from Election Day. While a September poll by Marist found Turek with an 8-point lead over Hinson, the gap has narrowed significantly between the two as Thursday's poll put Turek only 3 points ahead. Newsweek reached out to the campaigns for Turek and Hinson via email for comment on Thursday. Trump Schedules Iowa Rallies: What We Know Trump has planned two Iowa rallies in the coming weeks, aiming to boost Hinson's campaign against Turek. He has already endorsed Hinson, a U.S. Representative, for the Senate race. The Iowa rallies are the most recent in a series of campaign stops Trump has made ahead of the fast-approaching midterms as Republicans fight to maintain their majority in the U.S. Senate amid several tight races, including in Alaska and Texas. Trump is set to visit Iowa on October 22 and November 1. “I just got off the phone with President Trump," Republican Party of Iowa Chair Jeff Kaufmann said in a statement, according to a report by The Des Moines Register. "He told me that he will be in Iowa on October 22 and November 1. He is anxious for Iowans to hear his message before they vote. Stay tuned for further details." Times and venues for the rallies have not been announced. Ashley Hinson vs. Josh Turek: Latest Polls Two new polls came out this week assessing the race between Hinson and Turek. The polls were conducted by YouGov and Marist. The YouGov poll, which was held from October 6 to October 12, surveyed 2,245 likely voters and found that 47 percent planned to vote for Turek, giving him a 1-point lead over Hinson. According to the poll, 41 percent of respondents backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, compared with 52 percent who voted for Trump. Given Turek's edge, the results suggest he has won support from at least some voters who previously cast ballots for Trump. The Marist poll released on Thursday was held from October 8 to October 11 and surveyed 1,100 likely voters. Turek also leads Hinson in this poll, by 3 points. However, his lead over Hinson is much narrower than the last Marist poll, released in September, which gave him an 8-point lead. The study by Marist also showed improvement in Trump's approval ratings across Iowa. The September Marist poll showed that 41 percent of registered voters in Iowa approved of the job Trump was doing in office while 58 percent disapproved. A month later, 44 percent said they approved, while 53 percent disapproved. Biggest Issues Facing Iowa Voters Iowa voters are most concerned about the economy amid inflation and surging gas prices, according to a poll by The Economist that surveyed 650 likely voters on October 5 and October 6. The economy led top issues for voters, at 42 percent. It was followed by healthcare at 18 percent, threats to democracy at 10 percent and education at 8 percent. This year's midterm elections could flip control of the House and Senate as Republican candidates work to overcome widespread American concerns tied to the economy, inflation, rising fuel costs and the Iran war. Although Iowa has voted Republican in the Senate elections since 2008, the state has also had a history of voting for presidential candidates from both political parties, making the current political environment a competitive one. Trump won Iowa the last three election cycles, but before that, former President Barack Obama won the state twice. When Is Early Voting in Iowa? Early voting began in Iowa on October 14 and will continue through November 2. The election is November 3. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Kate Nalepinski and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Republican Ashley Hinson is gaining on Democrat Josh Turek in the race for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat, a new poll shows.
news.author: Anna Skinner

news.title: Kamala Harris Slams Biden and Trump Administrations for Failing to Act 'More Forcefully' Against Israel
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris said that both the Biden and Trump administrations failed to use U.S. leverage "sooner and more forcefully" to curb what she called the Israeli government's "horrific conduct" in the war in Gaza, RadarOnline.com has learned.

Speaking at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, Harris said the United States has at times fallen short of its "moral obligation to human rights and international law."Harris Calls Out Both Biden and Trump AdministrationsShe claimed that the alleged "failure" to act offered Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "a blank check."

The remarks came during a speech on American leadership, alliances, trade and the need to hold partners accountable for their share of global defense.

Harris argued that Washington must be willing to confront allies when their actions conflict with human rights and international law.Harris Wrote About Biden in MemoirThis isn't the first time she's shared criticism of the Biden administration's behavior regarding Israel.

In her 2025 memoir, 107 Days, she wrote that she had "pleaded with Joe" to extend the same empathy he showed Ukrainians to innocent Gazan civilians, but that his remarks on Palestinian suffering "came off as inadequate and forced."

She also wrote that Netanyahu had wanted Trump rather than Biden in the White House and had undermined Biden's loyalty to Israel.

During the 2024 campaign, Harris balanced calls for an immediate cease-fire and concern over civilian casualties with repeated statements that Israel had a right to defend itself.Harris Could Be Running Again in 2028Harris has said she has not decided whether she will run for president again in 2028. 

She leads or runs near the top of most early Democratic primary polls, though no major candidate has formally declared.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has said he would not run if Harris enters the race, calling a contest between two Californians a disadvantage for both.Voters Will Have Loaded Democratic PrimaryOther frequently discussed potential contenders include Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

Some progressive voters have cited the Biden administration's handling of the conflict as a reason they did not support Harris in 2024.

The White House and the Biden team have not publicly responded to her latest comments.
news.summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris said both the Biden and Trump administrations failed to use leverage 'sooner and more forcefully' with Israel.
news.author: Patrick Previty

news.title: NY Times Gushes Over Hillary Clinton’s ‘Next Act’ as Podcaster with Lefty Kara Swisher
news.text:
Wednesday’s New York Times Business section was blessed with “Hillary Clinton Starts Podcast On Election as Midterms Near.” The former First Lady, former U.S. Senator, and failed Democratic presidential nominee is forming a new podcast series for Vox Media with surly liberal tech journalist and podcaster Kara Swisher. The online headline came off more excited: “Hillary Clinton Steps to the Podcast Mic as Midterms Approach.” Was Kamala Harris unavailable?

Media reporter Benjamin Mullin is apparently easily impressed:

Hillary Clinton has rarely been far from the spotlight since her 2016 presidential bid. She has written best-selling books, taught at Columbia University and even tried her hand on Broadway as a producer for the Tony Award-winning musical “Suffs.”Her next act? Podcaster.With the midterm elections looming, Mrs. Clinton is preparing to make her voice heard on a new podcast series, called “High Stakes,” alongside the well-known technology journalist Kara Swisher. Starting Wednesday, Mrs. Clinton and Ms. Swisher will break down the race to control the House and the Senate in weekly episodes that run through mid-November.

Swisher, an Elon Musk/Jeff Bezos nemesis, is a regular subject at NewsBusters. She and Clinton are well-suited politically: Swisher was even a guest host on The View, temporarily joining the “cackling coven” this summer. But Mullin focused only on Clinton’s political opponents.

“I don’t think the stakes for the country and the world could be any higher,” Mrs. Clinton said in an interview with The New York Times last week. “If we don’t reverse this chaos and corruption and cruelty that is being visited upon us by this administration, we won’t recognize our country.”….The idea for the podcast came this spring at the sprawling home of former Atlantic owner David Bradley in Washington’s upscale Kalorama neighborhood. Ms. Swisher turned up to the soireé, which was being held for Mrs. Clinton, wearing a T-shirt and jeans and began peppering the former secretary of state with questions about a variety of topics — from the upcoming midterm elections to the continuing war in Ukraine.Ms. Swisher said she thought Mrs. Clinton’s answers were concise and intelligible, and Ms. Swisher wondered why Mrs. Clinton had not taken another swing at podcasting after her solo interview show, “You and Me Both With Hillary Clinton,” ended in 2023.The two got a test-run when Mrs. Clinton filled in for Ms. Swisher’s regular “Pivot” co-host, Scott Galloway, in August. Ms. Swisher wanted to give listeners the version of Mrs. Clinton she saw that evening, and persuaded her to team up.

There’s a distinct “Al Gore is loose and funny in private” feel to Swisher’s unchallenged praise.

“There’s a thing about the secretary, where it’s like, ‘Oh, if you knew her in the room, she’s so funny,’” Ms. Swisher said, adding, “We’re going to try to show you that room.”

After letting Clinton get another dig at Trump by joking she wouldn’t be selling “gold cellphones” on the podcast (“an apparent reference to Trump Mobile, the wireless network pushed by the Trump family”), Mullin nodded vaguely to the radical-left takeover of swathes of the Democratic Party.

Many voters are disenchanted with the Democratic establishment, which Mrs. Clinton still represents in many Americans’ minds. In light of that association, will Ms. Swisher’s audience want to hear from Mrs. Clinton?“Well, the first thing I’d say is, I’ve been called worse than ‘establishment,’” Mrs. Clinton joked. She added that many Democrats in contested races were now calling upon her to help campaign for votes and raise money. They are also asking her for ideas, she said.

Ideas for losing to Donald Trump?

“One of the things people try to do is split the Democratic Party, and that’s fine,” Mrs. Clinton said. “It’s fine to have differences, and it’s fine to argue. Nobody’s afraid of the argument.”

Except perhaps outlets like the New York Times, which won’t air out those Dem-on-Dem arguments in ways unflattering to the left-wing candidates.

news.title: Democratic senator accuses Biden administration of 'completely' chickening out on Supreme Court reform
news.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., called out the Biden administration on Wednesday for a lack of action taken on the Supreme Court and said they were "completely chicken" on it. The Lever's David Sirota asked Whitehouse about what "legitimate" resistance to the court might look like if a Democratic president believed the Supreme Court was "enabling an anti-democratic project." "Well, I think it starts with truth telling and I think the chief executive of the United States has the proverbial bully, the bulliest of all pulpits, and should be prepared to make the argument about what has gone wrong with the courts. The Biden administration was highly reluctant to do that. They completely chickened out. Biden set up that lame committee commission on the Supreme Court and then squelched both Judge Gertner and Professor Tribe when they wanted to describe some of the actual problems at the court so that they couldn't even get that into the report," Whitehouse said. LIBERAL JUSTICE HAMMERS SUPREME COURT FOR FAST-TRACKING EMERGENCY DOCKET CASES He continued, "The Biden people didn't want to go there. They were completely chicken about all that. They wanted no part of that. And it — really wasn't until the very end, in his last speech after he and Harris had both lost that Biden seemed to have at least somewhat awakened to the fact that the Supreme Court had a real integrity problem." FLASHBACK: DEM SENATOR EMBROILED IN CONFLICT OF INTEREST ROW TARGETED SCOTUS IN ETHICS CRUSADE Nancy Gertner and Laurence Tribe served on former President Biden's Presidential Commission on the Supreme Court. Gertner and Tribe wrote an op-ed in The Washington Post in December 2021, calling for adding more justices to the court after the commission ultimately took no position on adding more justices. DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION Gertner and Tribe were two of the 34 members of the commission, and wrote in The Washington Post, "We now believe that Congress must expand the size of the Supreme Court and do so as soon as possible. We did not come to this conclusion lightly." Whitehouse has been a proponent of Supreme Court ethics legislation as he has argued that the Court has been captured by "right-wing billionaires and special interests." GAVIN NEWSOM EXPRESSES 'OPENNESS' TO PACKING SCOTUS, CALLS ELECTORAL COLLEGE SYSTEM 'PERVERTED' Former Vice President Kamala Harris called for expanding the Supreme Court during an interview on Wednesday, among other big institutional changes, which included Electoral College reform. "The work that we can do about winning back the House and the Senate is going to be on a number of things. For example, I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court. We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States," Harris told podcast host Keke Palmer on her "Baby, This is Keke Palmer" podcast. "I believe that we should be pushing for what is possible around changing the Electoral College. Right?" HARRIS LABELED 'INSTITUTIONAL ARSONIST' FOR PLAN TO FUNDAMENTALLY TRANSFORM SCOTUS AND ELECTORAL COLLEGE She also called for pursuing statehood for Washington, D.C., as well as Puerto Rico. Her comments come days after her 2024 vice presidential running mate, Gov. Tim Walz, warned of a reckoning among Democrats if the party fails to deliver on structural change and promises should they take back Congress and potentially the presidency in 2028. "The odds of Democrats changing the composition of the Supreme Court through a constitutional amendment are near zero, while changing it via statutory legislation (such as expanding the number of seats or imposing term limits) would be extraordinarily difficult. It is a pipe dream. A fantasy. It’s nothing more than something to get their base excited about," Northwestern adjunct law professor Andrew Stoltmann told Fox News Digital in a statement. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE He continued, "A constitutional amendment requires a two-thirds vote in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, followed by ratification by three-fourths (38 of 50) of state legislatures. Given the deep divides, politically, this is almost impossible. It’s almost silly for Democrats to be arguing that this is a realistic possibility." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Biden's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
news.summary: Sheldon Whitehouse said the Biden administration was "completely chicken" on Supreme Court reform, while Kamala Harris now pushes court expansion.

news.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle flaunted her nudes album to me... with each man's Amex card next to his compromising photo: KENNEDY spills every sordid secret from their Fox News days
news.text:
Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle's spectacular collapse is one of the most predictable career implosions in modern American history.

In the age of Hillary Clinton, Kamala Harris and Katie Zacharia (too soon?), that's really saying something.

I wasn't shocked by the Daily Mail reporting that Kimmy G was under investigation by the State Department Inspector General or when a random Republican donor claimed that she begged him for $100,000 to cover her American Express bill.

I worked with Guilfoyle for years at Fox News. By the time I joined the network in 2012, Kim was already something of a rising star, having started as a legal analyst and climbing the ranks to co-host The Five.

She is insanely charming and we first bonded over our shared disdain for her ex-husband, California's Greasy Gavin Newsom.

'No offense,' I told her. 'I think your ex is a douchebag.'

'I love you and now I know why,' she replied.

Though, the more I got to know Kimberly, the less comfortable I felt around her.

I can't tell you the number of people who have insane stories about this woman, most of which cannot be published because they'd either be legally problematic or make you hurl. But I can say that she's a status-chasing monster always – it seems to me – planning her next move.

I eventually developed a Golden Rule with her: Never, ever, share anything in confidence with Kimberly unless you wanted everyone in her orbit to know about it. In that sense, I treated her like a publicist. If there was something that I needed the world to know, I'd whisper it to her and make her swear not to tell a soul. 

Then, there was the manipulation and the unrelenting narcissism.

Kimberly claimed to me – and whomever else was within earshot – that just about everyone at Fox News was in love with her and wanted to sleep with her, especially the women.

One unsettling night, she asked me to meet her at her apartment, which was around the corner from my home, so that we could Uber together to a mutual friend's birthday party.

She answered the door in a black, push-up corset and thigh-high stockings, and purred: 'You like what you see?'

No, I did not. Her weave looked like horsehair and her legs like bendable Ball Park Franks.

I eked out a sheepish, 'You're in great shape.'

Honestly, I was scared of her and it felt like a trap.

I imagined that if I had said, 'Geez Kim, you're so hot you're making me rethink this boring old heterosexuality!' she'd go around the office telling everyone that I wanted to be her Sugar Mama.

Reading that she was allegedly trying to milk Republican donor Eric Deters for one hundred grand on the eve of Senate confirmation (Guilfoyle denies the claim), I just shook my head and thought, 'That's our gal!'

She's always had a thing for Amex.

While at Fox News, Kimberly dated a man who she referred to as 'Lex Luthor.' According to her, he was a lovesick cash cow, who would seemingly do anything to make her happy. Kimberly showed me and several of our friends pictures of his Amex black card – front and back. The images were matched with a corresponding picture of the card holder's private parts.

There were at least three sets of these credit card-penis pairings. 

She was infamously branded 'Seabiscuit' and the 'USO' inside Fox News. I won't go into the origins of those nicknames, but they were related to her reputation knowing many, many men. 

In fact, Kimberly talked about sex so cavalierly that she made Samantha from Sex and the City seem like Greta Thunberg.

When the initial allegations of sexual assault against former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes started gushing out into the media, Kimberly called me just after six in the morning and demanded that I pledge my loyalty to Ailes and his wife. Terrified that I'd be swung if he survived the onslaught of allegations, I sheepishly went along with it just to get her off the phone.

Eventually, her time at Fox News came to an end amid sexual harassment allegations which included claims she showed a young female assistant – you guessed it – pictures of a conquests's nether regions. Guilfoyle has denied the allegations.

But Kimberly rebounded, hitching up with Donald Trump Jr and launching the next phase of her illustrious career.

Even now, I get a lump in my throat writing about her, because for all the allegations, the stories and the implosion of her ambassadorship, I'm not so sure we've seen the end of Kimberly Guilfoyle.

I have to ponder how has she survived this long? Is she a soulless opportunist whose life is one big hustle, a bedazzled con-artist who simply brachiates from one mark to the next, hoping eventually she hits the jackpot?

We'll see if this frisky cat has finally exhausted all her nine lives, or if she'll miraculously rub up against yet another scratching post to save her fur.

If the Democrats win control of the House of Representatives in the midterms, I expect that they'll call Kim to tell all. She has made herself a laughably easy target. Perhaps Lex Luthor's former girlfriend turns out to be the biggest villain in Trumpland!

But for now, I wouldn't count her out.

I'll just say: Kimberly, you looked fantastic in those thigh-highs.
news.summary: One unsettling night, she asked me to meet her at her apartment, which was around the corner from my home, so that we could Uber together to a mutual friend's birthday party.

news.title: At the Races: Seeing red in Minnesota?
news.text:
Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the CQ Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Mary Ellen McIntire, Daniela Altimari and Niels Lesniewski

Campaigning some thousand miles away in Ohio this week, President Donald Trump urged Minnesotans to vote for Republican Michele Tafoya, who is seeking to flip the blue-leaning state’s open Senate seat. 

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee, quickly sought to capitalize on the endorsement, while Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter, didn’t do much to tout it.

“Look, this campaign is about bringing all Minnesotans together, whether they voted for President Trump or whether they voted for Kamala Harris,” the Republican said at a Tuesday news conference, according to the Minnesota Reformer.

Tafoya’s lukewarm reaction is reflective of the line she is walking in a state that backed Harris in 2024 but that Senate Republicans see as a rare pickup opportunity this year. Recent polls have shown Tafoya trailing Flanagan by single digits. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales shifted the race rating in Republicans’ favor earlier this month, from Likely Democratic to Lean Democratic. 

But the Gopher State hasn’t elected a Republican to statewide office in two decades, and in a year when the GOP faces competitive Senate elections in several deep-red states, the party is yet to make a full-throttle play for Minnesota as they have in Michigan and New Hampshire. 

Senate Majority Leader John Thune campaigned for Tafoya earlier this month, and Sen. Tim Scott, who heads Senate Republicans' campaign arm, continues to cite the polls showing a close race. 

But Republican groups like the Senate Leadership Fund and entities affiliated with Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC have not invested in the state so far. Similarly, top Democratic outside groups have also not engaged in the race.

Still, Republicans believe the major fraud scandal that rocked the state last year and pushed Gov. Tim Walz to drop his reelection bid has created a vulnerability for his No. 2, though Walz has maintained that Flanagan was not responsible.

Tafoya and Flanagan are set to meet for a debate Friday.

Starting gate

Roll Call on the road: Four House races in Pennsylvania could help decide control of the chamber this year. One of them is the contest for the 8th District, where Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, like other Democratic candidates across the country, is leaning into anti-corruption messaging as she takes on Republican freshman Rob Bresnahan Jr., who is emphasizing the times when he’s broken with his party. Mary Ellen and Roll Call photojournalist Tom Williams joined editor-in-chief Jason Dick on the latest "Political Theater" podcast to talk about their recent trip to the Keystone State, including how Sha Na Na frontman and Social Security advocate Jon “Bowzer” Bauman is trying to fire up Democratic voters.

Playing hardball: The House Freedom Caucus is poised to lose several stalwarts after this year, but a new crop of leaders stands ready to steer the hard-line conservative bloc and shape the Republican policy agenda – no matter which party controls the chamber.

Purple politics: After trending red over the past decade, Iowa is battleground territory once again, with the Hawkeye State playing host to pivotal races for the Senate and House. Student journalists from USC Annenberg Media crisscrossed the state recently, talking to voters and politicians and found an “engaged electorate frustrated with partisan politics and hoping for candidates who will work on local issues.” 

Omar targeted: A federal search of Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington residence sent political shockwaves this week, and some experts worry it could set a wider precedent for how the Trump administration handles investigations of other Democrats, our colleague Michael Macagnone reports. The probe, which reportedly centers on immigration paperwork that Omar used to secure legal status and ultimately U.S. citizenship, has also put a spotlight on the agency that carried out the raid, Roll Call’s Paul M. Krawzak and Jacob Fulton reported.

Exit interview: Senate Minority Whip Richard J. Durbin, who is retiring after this year, spoke to Roll Call’s Nina Heller about his more-than-four decades in Congress, including how “painful” it is to leave with his DREAM Act yet to become law. Niels also looked back at the Illinois Democrat’s influence on another matter: the business of baseball.

First ladies: Two senators and a House delegate are among several women who could be elected as the first female governors of their states or territory next month.

No to 2028: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff pledged to serve a full six-year term if the Democrat is reelected next month, saying on the debate stage this week that he had “zero interest” in running for president. 

Triage time: Punchbowl News reported that groups tied to Trump’s MAGA Inc. have pulled ad money from the districts of Democratic Reps. Tom Suozzi of New York and Susie Lee of Nevada. Congressional Leadership Fund, the top House GOP super PAC, and other groups have reportedly also redirected funds from the races of vulnerable Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa and Thomas H. Kean Jr. of New Jersey and canceled reservations meant to boost the challengers to Democrats Henry Cuellar of Texas, Greg Landsman of Ohio and Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan. 

#FL27: Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar, who famously broke with Trump on immigration last month, touted an endorsement from Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella as she seeks a fourth term representing her Miami district, home to significant Colombian population. While de la Espriella is a U.S. citizen, House Foreign Affairs ranking member Gregory W. Meeks said his “decision to involve himself in an American election while serving as the leader of Colombia” jeopardizes bipartisan support for the Washington-Bogota alliance. 

More endorsements: The political arm of the moderate Blue Dog Coalition rolled out more endorsements of Democrats running in deep-red terrain: Nancy Lacore in South Carolina’s 1st District; Dwayne Romero in Colorado’s 3rd; Don Coover in Kansas’ 2nd; Paul Barringer in North Carolina’s 13th; Eileen Laubacher in Colorado’s 4th; Amanda Marie Green in Florida’s 2nd; and Zack Mullock in New Jersey’s 2nd. In Colorado, GOP former Rep. Ken Buck endorsed and cut a video for Democrat Phil Weiser, who’s running for governor. And in New Hampshire, Don Bolduc, the state’s 2022 Republican nominee for Senate, endorsed Democrat Chris Pappas’ campaign for Senate against GOP former Sen. John E. Sununu.

Trump on the trail: The president returns to the campaign circuit Friday, with a visit to Georgia, followed by trips to Kentucky on Saturday, Kansas on Monday and North Carolina on Tuesday. Local Republican officials in South Carolina say the president will visit their state on Wednesday, while the Iowa GOP chairman says Trump plans to visit the state twice before Election Day, including next Thursday. 

Former POTII on the trail: Former President Barack Obama, whose increasing campaign activities we reported on last week, also plans to campaign next week in Ohio, a state he carried twice while running for president. Former President Bill Clinton also plans to hit the trail, rallying on Tuesday with former Rep. David Jolly, the Republican-turned-Democrat running for Florida governor.

Nathan’s notes

While dozens of House Republicans are sweating their reelection bids, the party’s biggest challenge lies with GOP-held open seats, according to Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections. 

Republican nominees in these districts often don’t have established profiles to help carry them through a challenging election for their party, Nathan writes. 

What we’re reading

AI mystery: The pro-AI Leading the Future super PAC has raised enormous sums to promote candidates on both sides of the aisle. Wired looked at a mysterious group of Nevada-based LLCs that are behind the PAC, which election watchdogs say are shell companies created to “to mask the identities of strategists, consultants, and production companies who are working with Leading the Future.”

The new Steny: Politico caught up with House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, whom some Democrats say will restore “a sense of order” to the chamber if the party wins the majority this year. 

Dark money drama: Outside money is fueling a state Senate race in western Pennsylvania between the Republican incumbent and an independent candidate who is running on a populist message, Spotlight PA reports.

Weird and wacky: State Navigate examines some of the quirky candidates, bizarre controversies and messy feuds playing out in legislative contests around the nation.

Stop the press: Candidates across the country have attempted to restrict press access to their campaigns, The Washington Sun reports, the latest being Republican Rep. Andy Harris, who tried to bar a reporter from recording him during a media availability after a candidate forum in Maryland. 

Internal affairs: A flurry of partisan polls – mostly from Democrats – offer a window into the expanding House battleground, but, as the National Journal reports, they could also be providing a flawed view of the fight for control of the chamber.

The count: 96 percent

That’s how often the most endangered House Republicans have collectively sided with Trump this year when it comes to floor votes on which he took a public position.

The group includes 16 Republicans who are running for reelection in races that Inside Elections rates as Toss-ups or favoring Democrats. Three of them were aligned with Trump's stance on all such votes: Pennsylvania’s Ryan Mackenzie, Ohio’s Max Miller and Wisconsin’s Derrick Van Orden.

Our colleague Ryan Kelly has more on the voting records of these vulnerable Republicans, including how they may or may not have shifted from 2025.

Key race: #WA03

Candidates: Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Pérez has twice been elected from Washington’s 3rd District, both times defeating Republican Joe Kent, who trafficked in conspiracy theories and had ties to white nationalists. But this year she faces GOP state Senate Minority Leader John Braun, a business owner and retired Navy captain whose moderate record and less flamboyant style stand in contrast to Kent.

Why it matters: The Southwest Washington district is a classic swing seat that has flipped between the two parties since the mid-1990s. Trump carried the district by 3 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections, which rates the race between Gluesenkamp Pérez and Braun a Toss-up.

Cash dash: Gluesenkamp Pérez reported raising $6.3 million through the middle of July, compared with $2.2 million for Braun. Outside groups affiliated with both parties are also spending heavily in the race, the bulk of it on the Republican side. Congressional Leadership Fund, the top House GOP super PAC, and No Going Back PAC Inc., which is aligned with Trump’s political operation, jointly spent more than $6 million on Braun’s behalf through last week. The pro-Democratic House Majority PAC had spent nearly $2 million.

Backers: Gluesenkamp Pérez, a co-chair of the moderate Blue Dog Coalition, has the backing of EMILY’s List, the Latino Victory Fund and a host of local labor organizations. Braun, who has Trump’s endorsement, is a member of the NRCC’s MAGA Majority program, which provides promising recruits with additional resources and support.

What they’re saying: Gluesenkamp Pérez has cast herself as a pragmatist willing to buck her party, even when it angers Democratic leaders, while attacking Braun as a Trump loyalist. She owns an auto repair shop with her husband and has championed vocational education and right-to-repair laws popular with rural voters. Braun has highlighted his efforts in the Legislature to fight a state tax on household income exceeding $1 million per year as well as his support for the tax-cutting provisions of Trump’s spending bill. He has derided Gluesenkamp Pérez as a D.C. insider who hasn’t accomplished much in her four years in the House.

Terrain: Washington’s 3rd District is geographically and politically diverse. Stretching along the state’s southern border, it includes Vancouver, a blue-leaning city that’s part of the Portland, Ore., metropolitan area, along with more conservative rural communities.

Wild card: Support from Trump could undercut Braun’s image as a moderate and hurt him in a midterm cycle where the president’s national approval rating is hovering in the 30s. Progressive voters will be crucial to Gluesenkamp Pérez’s reelection chances. She drew their ire over her votes for an early iteration of Trump’s voting bill, now known as the SAVE America Act, and for a measure that would require parental consent if students change their pronouns in the classroom. Democrat Brent Hennrich, an underfunded outsider who finished third running to Gluesenkamp Pérez’s left in the August all-party primary, is not backing her in the general election. He told the Washington State Standard he’d be fine with Braun winning though he wouldn’t vote for him.

Fundraising reports covering the third quarter of the year through Sept. 30 are due with the Federal Election Commission by the end of Thursday.

news.title: Megyn Kelly Reveals Why She Wants Democrat Journalist Don Lemon to Run for President
news.text:
Megyn Kelly said she believes Don Lemon should consider running for president after the former CNN anchor revealed he has thought about entering politics, RadarOnline can report.

During her October 13 episode of The Megyn Kelly Show, Kelly argued that Lemon’s journalism background would not prevent him from pursuing public office and compared his intellect with prominent Democratic figures, including Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.Megyn Kelly’s Endorsement: 'I Think He Should Do It'Reacting to Lemon's comments, Kelly said, "OK, I'm going to shock you," before adding, "I think he should do it. I actually think he should do it."

Former Fox News personality Kelly also argued that Lemon's experience as a journalist could translate into a career in public service. 

She questioned whether Harris and Biden were significantly more intelligent than Lemon and said he could "match wits against Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez just fine."Better Than Donald Trump?Lemon previously said that fans regularly ask whether he would run for office. 

He admitted he has "thought about it," claimed he would be better at the job than President Donald Trump, and estimated there was a 65-70 percent chance he would run for office at some point in his life.

Lemon and Kelly began on friendly terms in the mid-2010s. In a September 2016 tribute, Kelly wrote in the publication that their first meeting years earlier was "the beginning of a beautiful friendship."News Media FrenemiesThey texted during commercial breaks about news and guests, shared personal common ground (both lost their fathers young), and she noted their outsider positions at the time. 

She called him bold, easygoing, and introspective. Lemon has later acknowledged they were once friendly. However, the relationship shifted into open criticism and a public feud as their careers diverged. 

Kelly repeatedly criticized Lemon's comments and behavior toward women, including his 2023 remarks that Nikki Haley was not "in her prime," which she labeled sexist. 

A major flashpoint came in February 2025 when Kelly, 55, celebrated Joy Reid's MSNBC show cancellation. 

Lemon responded with a lengthy rant, telling Kelly to "go f-ck yourself," calling her a "troll" and "racist," and referencing her past controversies.

The 60-year-old continued personal attacks later, including 2025 comments describing Kelly as "chopped" due to what he called the "MAGA look," saying she "looks trans" and is "clockable."

Despite the hostility, limited moments of restraint occurred. In April 2023, after CNN fired Lemon, Kelly called the reported handling "classless" if true and said he had a right to complain.Not the First Reporter to Turn Presidential CandidateLemon’s potential presidential ambitions would not be unprecedented. Several media professionals have sought the presidency, including newspaper editors, publishers, and journalists who later entered politics.

Horace Greeley, the founder and longtime editor of the New-York Tribune, was one of the most influential journalists of the 19th century. 

The Liberal Republican Party nominated him for president in 1872, and the Democratic Party also endorsed him to challenge incumbent Republican President Ulysses S. Grant. 

Grant won reelection in a landslide on November 5, 1872. Greeley died on November 29, before the Electoral College formally cast its votes.

Steve Forbes, the publisher of Forbes magazine, also pursued the presidency, running for the Republican nomination in 1996 and 2000. 

Sarah Palin, meanwhile, worked as a sports reporter and broadcaster in Alaska before becoming the Republican vice-presidential nominee alongside John McCain in 2008.
news.summary: Megyn Kelly explained why she wants former CNN anchor Don Lemon to run for president, sharing her take on the journalist's political ambitions and potential candidacy.

news.title: Trump Shoots Down Report Claiming He Is Considering Replacing Susie Wiles
news.text:
President Donald Trump on Thursday dismissed a Politico report claiming he is weighing replacing White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, calling the outlet “TOTAL FAKE NEWS.”

Politico reported in Playbook that Trump is eyeing potential replacements for Wiles, but in a statement to the publication, Trump stressed Wiles has his full confidence and blasted the outlet:

“TOTAL FAKE NEWS Politico doesn’t care about facts, integrity, or honest journalism — it’s why I kicked them out of the White House!” the president said. “Susie Wiles is my loyal and longest serving Chief of Staff — there is a reason for that. She has been with me since the beginning, is my trusted advisor, and has my COMPLETE confidence. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Politico, citing anonymous sources, wrote that Trump is considering White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, New York Yankees President Randy Levine, former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-CA), Director of National Intelligence Bill Pulte, and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as candidates to succeed Wiles, despite the president’s dismissal of the narrative.

Wiles has served as chief of staff through the first 20 months of Trump’s second term. Before that, she co-managed his wildly successful 2024 campaign in which he won all seven swing states and the popular vote against former Vice President Kamala Harris.

She is the first woman to ever serve as chief of staff for a president and was ranked 66th on Forbes’ “The Most Powerful 100 Women in the World.”

In March, Trump announced that Wiles was diagnosed with breast cancer. Wiles continued to serve in her capacity essentially full-time following the diagnosis, and in September, she announced she was “cancer free.”

“Some personal news I’m grateful to share. After a medical appointment at the Mayo Clinic this week, my pathology results came back clear,” said Wiles. “I am cancer free.”

“Thank you to my family, friends, doctors, and everyone who prayed for me, checked in, and supported me along the way,” she continued. “A special thank you to President Trump for his unwavering support. I am deeply grateful and will continue to work to advance his America First Agenda.”
news.summary:
President Donald Trump on Thursday dismissed a Politico report claiming he is looking to replace White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, calling the outlet “TOTAL FAKE NEWS."

Comcast donated $7.5 million to fund President Donald Trump’s new White House ballroom, raising questions of whether the contribution was meant to curry favor with the administration.

A list obtained by The Washington Post revealed all the major donors to the project. Comcast had already been identified as a contributor, though the amount of the donation wasn’t disclosed. At the time, the company had several matters before the government, including investigations into its diversity, equity and inclusion programs, treatment of local broadcast affiliates and Kamala Harris’ appearance on NBC’s Saturday Night Live. There were also rumblings of a potential Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition.

Total donations to the 89,000-square-foot, two-story ballroom totaled $333 million, according to the report. Familiar names in Hollywood that contributed: Apple, which donated $25 million, Google, which donated $22 million through a settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against YouTube, and Amazon, which donated $5 million. Separately, Dish Network chairman Charlie Ergen gave $25 million, with former Marvel CEO Ike Perlmutter’s nonprofit giving more than $20 million.

After Comcast was identified as a donor last year, lawmakers raised concerns of the company trying to secure favorable treatment form the government related to merger reviews or enforcement actions. They pointed to a potential merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, which would’ve require a greenlight from competition enforcers.

“This interest in favorable action from the Trump Administration creates the potential for a quid- pro-quo exchange of a contribution to the ballroom for regulatory or other favors from the federal government,” stated the letter to Comcast CEO Brian Roberts. “That risk appears particularly acute amid allegations of this Administration’s politicized decision-making in antitrust cases, not based on law and the interest of the public but based on political favors.”

It’s unknown whether the FCC’s inquiries into Comcast concluded with penalties or findings of wrongdoing.

Last month, the Supreme Court allowed construction of the ballroom to continue, pausing a ruling from a federal judge halting the project. The building is believed to be one of Trump’s top priorities.

news.title: How Adam Hamilton plans on winning Kansas' Senate race
news.text:
The most surprising battleground race is shaping up in ruby red Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932.

But Rev. Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, could buck that trend.

He's challenging incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall – and the two candidates are neck-and-neck in recent polling.

"I think Kansas has a chance to send a message to America to say, look, we got to come together, we got to work together," Hamilton said in an interview with ABC News' Jon Karl that aired Sunday. "I'll only get elected with Republicans voting for me."

President Donald Trump handily won the Sunflower State by 16 points in 2024, but a recent New York Times/Siena poll found 55% of likely voters disapprove of his job as president.

Hamilton, who brands himself an "independent-minded" Democrat, said he's both a liberal and a conservative.

"I'm proud to be a Democrat, but what matters to me more than the letter behind your name is who you are, what you stand for, your character, and I think there's a lot of people like that in our state," Hamilton told Karl.

After the ABC News interview aired, Marshall responded on social media, calling Hamilton "the ultimate snake oil salesman" and claiming the pastor, despite his messaging as being a moderate, has been "a proud donor to Obama, Biden, and Kamala Harris."

The megachurch pastor has been affiliated with both parties in the past and was a registered Democrat during the Obama administration. He was appointed by President Obama to serve on the President's Advisory Council on Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships.

Throughout the Senate campaign, Marshall has called Hamilton "too woke."

But on issues like transgender rights, Hamilton said he believes there are two genders and that men should not be competing in women's sports, even though "people might identify in different ways."

"The president has taken a group of people that represent a very tiny minority of people who are bullied and picked on and harassed, and he's tried to make them a campaign issue," Hamilton said. "He's trying to use them in order to somehow make the case that people should be afraid of trans people as well as Democrats, and I think that again is pathetic."

While Marshall links him to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Hamilton has expressed a willingness to push back against top Democratic leadership if elected.

"I get asked, 'If Chuck Schumer tells you to do something, what are you going to do?' And my answer is, 'If it's good for Kansas, I'm all in. But if it's bad for Kansas, I'm a hard no,'" Hamilton said.

Money, money, money

Bob Beatty, the political science chair and professor at the University of Washburn, attributed the pastor's strong communication and fundraising skills to his experience leading the Church of the Resurrection in Leawood. He said Hamilton "is like a gift from the political gods to the Democrats."

But as the polls tighten, outside spending is now pouring in. The top Senate Republican and Democrat-aligned super PACS are spending millions to boost their preferred candidates.

"I can't remember a race here in Kansas that's become so ... dirty ... so ugly," said Philip Perry, a 66-year-old rancher and three-time Trump voter based in the northeastern city of Oskaloosa.

Perry, a former president of the Kansas Livestock Association, said he's been "disappointed" by the current administration. The group withheld an endorsement in the Senate race this year.

"To hear from Washington that they're going to do something to lower the price of our product, that really kind of hits home, especially when we supported this administration so much," he said.

Perry said he has shaken hands with Hamilton in church and praised him for doing "a tremendous job of bringing people together in that Kansas City metro area."

But he said that Marshall has done "a good enough job" and will vote for the incumbent.

In the home stretch, the biggest challenge for Republicans is winning the battle for the narrative, according to Rob Fillion, the executive director for the state's GOP party.

"One of the biggest problems we're seeing is somewhat confusion," Fillion said. "Almost every ad is a negative ad, and so I think both the Republican Party and the Democrat Party are guilty of this. They have voters not knowing what and who they're voting for."

He told ABC News he expects the race will be tighter than in the past given it's a midterm year. Marshall will likely prevail, he added.

The senator has held few public events since a town hall meeting in March 2025, when he walked away from voters angry about federal job cuts. Marshall appeared at stops as part of the Kansas GOP's statewide bus tour this week.

In September, Vice President JD Vance held a rally in Kansas, what Hamilton considered "a great compliment that the second most powerful man in America came here to try to save Roger Marshall."

The Iran war has driven up the price of gas, diesel fuel and fertilizer, hurting farmers already grappling with uncertainty over the president's tariff policies.

It's affecting voters like Steve Bowlin, a 70-year-old third-generation farmer based in Olathe who sits on the board of the Johnson County Farm Bureau.

Bowlin, who grows produce, said he worries whether his decades-old family farm will survive. "People don't understand what it takes to put food on the table," Bowlin said.

He told ABC News he does not believe that Washington is hearing his concerns. And the president's endorsement of Sen. Roger Marshall is not a factor when it comes to his vote this fall.

"I don't care who he endorses," Bowlin said. "I want somebody that is talking for the American farmer."

Marshall says Republicans are 'coming home'

In a state that has voted for both Republicans and Democrats to the governorship, Hamilton is seeking to build a large coalition.

Two former Republican governors -- Bill Graves and Mike Hayden -- are backing Hamilton. So is Marshall's former GOP primary opponent, Arch Naramore.

Former GOP Gov. Sam Brownback has endorsed Marshall.

On Friday, Marshall toured a radar manufacturing plant with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. He brushed off concerns about Republican support for his opponent.

"I think it’s a very finite amount of people," Marshall told ABC News. "What I see across the state is Republicans coming home."

That could be the case, but some Republicans like Bruce Bratman, who voted for Trump three times, told ABC News he is knocking doors for Hamilton.

At a packed theater in Hutchinson, in a county Trump carried by about 34 percentage points in the last presidential election, some Republican and independents turned out for Hamilton.

"I think it'd be crazy not to elect him," said Laura Shea, an unaffiliated voter. "I think we'd be crazy if we elected the representative we have now, who I don't feel, and a lot of people don't feel, is representing us. We don't see him from the things he does or doesn't do."

Ed Berger, a former Republican state senator who represented Hutchinson, also pledged support for Hamilton.

"Our current senator is not representing Kansas. He's not standing up to policies that hurt Kansans everyday," Berger told ABC News. "The senator should represent his constituency and have the courage to stand up to the executive branch."

Joshua Farr, a self-described constitutional conservative, went to the Hutchinson event to learn more about the candidate.

"I might vote for Hamilton this time. It's just, I don't really like Democrats. Democrats tend to be more liberal and I'm not that liberal," Farr said.

At a campaign event held at a college chapel in Lindsborg, Hamilton led the crowd in a hymn and did not mention his opponent by name.

"Most of us around here are not actually enemies. If we're liberals or conservatives, we just see the world differently," Hamilton said.

news.title: Kamala Harris slams Biden & Trump over Gaza war, says US should have acted ‘sooner, more forcefully’
news.text: Former US vice president Kamala Harris has criticised both the Joe Biden and Donald Trump administrations for failing to use Washington’s influence to control Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, saying the US should have acted “sooner and more forcefully”.Speaking at the Asan Memorial Lecture organised by the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul, South Korea, on Wednesday, Harris described the failure to use American leverage to curb the Israeli government’s conduct during the war in Gaza as a major shortcoming of US policy.“Most recently, the failure to use our leverage to curtail the Israeli government’s horrific conduct in the war in Gaza, both under the current administration, which offers [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu a blank check, and our administration before, where we should have acted sooner and more forcefully,” Harris said.Her remarks amounted to a criticism of the Biden administration, under which she served as vice president, as well as the current Trump administration, which she accused of giving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unconditional support.Republican Jewish Coalition hits back at HarrisHarris’s comments drew criticism from the Republican Jewish Coalition, which described her position as “unsurprising”. The group cited her absence from Netanyahu’s 2024 address to the US Congress and her opposition to legislation targeting the boycott, divestment and sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel.The organisation also criticised Harris for calling for a halt to Israeli military operations in Rafah, a city in southern Gaza, and for agreeing with a student in 2021 who accused Israel of “ethnic genocide”.Warren Kinsella, an attorney and author who worked on Harris’s 2024 presidential campaign, also expressed disappointment over her latest remarks, writing on social media that he was “ashamed to have worked with her”.Harris says US foreign policy needs a rethinkBeyond the Gaza conflict, Harris spoke about the changing nature of American power and the need to rethink traditional approaches to foreign policy.She argued that economic innovation, markets, minerals and semiconductor technology were becoming increasingly important sources of global influence, alongside military strength.“Coming out of world wars, and into the Cold War, military might was the primary source of power,” she said. “But now more than ever, economic innovation, markets and minerals, chips and computers, have greater influence.”Harris also stressed the importance of strengthening US alliances, pointing to closer ties among China, Russia, Iran and North Korea as a development Washington and its partners needed to monitor.Harris puts 2026 midterms ahead of 2028 presidential raceHarris expressed confidence that Democrats would win the November 2026 midterm elections but sidestepped a direct question about whether she planned to run for president in 2028.“2028, from my perspective, doesn’t matter if we don’t win 2026,” she said, indicating that the immediate priority for Democrats was the upcoming congressional elections.You use AI every day. news.title: Megyn Kelly encourages Don Lemon to run for president: ‘I’m going to shock you’
news.text:
Conservative podcaster Megyn Kelly offered a surprising endorsement of media rival Don Lemon, who has repeatedly floated the idea of running for president in the 2028 election. 

During her podcast “The Megyn Kelly Show” Tuesday, Kelly, 55, argued Lemon, 60, should follow through on a presidential run – arguing he can’t be any worse than former Vice President Kamala Harris or former President Joe Biden. 

“I’m going to shock you. I think he should do it. I actually think he should do it,” Kelly said.

“First of all, it’s not a dealbreaker that he has spent his life as a journalist. I mean, you could absolutely parlay that into a career in public service.

“Second of all, do you really think Kamala Harris is a lot smarter than Don Lemon? Do you?” Kelly said. “I know she was at least a lawyer, she was an attorney general for the state of California – [but] no, I don’t believe so.

“Do you think Joe Biden was? I don’t. Are we so enamored with our public officials now, we don’t think somebody like Don Lemon could do it? Honestly! I’m not.” 

Lemon – a former CNN anchor who now hosts his own podcast – has said he’s “serious” about running in the 2028 presidential election, insisting he’d be a “really good” commander-in-chief. He has also suggested using his podcast to campaign.

“I actually think, yeah, he could match wits against AOC [Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a possible 2028 election contender] just fine,” Kelly continued. “And will he do it from his podcasting booth? That would be interesting to watch.” 

“All I can say is it would certainly give us a lot to talk about, so I encourage him and I’m rooting for him.” 

Lemon was fired from CNN in April 2023 after 17 years with the network, following accusations of his sexist and “diva-like behavior.” 

The controversial morning news host has since been working as an independent journalist, hosting his own podcast, “The Don Lemon Show,” on YouTube and other streaming platforms. 

In January, Lemon was arrested for allegedly joining a group of anti-ICE activists who stormed a church service in Minnesota. 

He pleaded not guilty to federal civil rights charges, arguing he was acting in his capacity as an independent journalist by covering the church protest.

Kelly – a former TV personality on NBC News and Fox News – was fired from NBC News in 2018 after she defended the use of blackface in Halloween costumes.

She apologized to staffers and viewers, but her show, “Megyn Kelly Today,” was promptly canceled.
news.summary: “I’m going to shock you. I think he should do it. I actually think he should do it,” Kelly said.

news.title: Kamala Harris criticizes Biden, Trump administrations for not acting ‘more forcefully’ against Israel
news.text:
Former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris criticized the Biden and Trump administrations on Wednesday for failing to use U.S. leverage to curb Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, saying Washington should have acted “sooner and more forcefully.”

“Most recently, the failure to use our leverage to curtail the Israeli government’s horrific conduct in the war in Gaza, both under the current administration, which offers [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu a blank check, and our administration before, where we should have acted sooner and more forcefully,” Harris said while speaking at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul, South Korea.

 Israeli soldiers and tanks from the IDF’s 252nd Division operate in the northern Gaza Strip, Wednesday, June 3, 2026. IDF

The Republican Jewish Coalition called Harris’s remarks “unsurprising,” citing her absence from Netanyahu’s 2024 address to Congress and her opposition to legislation targeting the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement.

The group also criticized Harris for calling for a halt to Israeli military operations in Rafah, where the Israel Defense Forces later found and rescued hostages, and for agreeing with a student in 2021 who accused Israel of “ethnic genocide.”

news.title: US teen held over Hindu temple attack plot: Is anti-Indian racism rising?  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St
news.text:
A 19-year-old American who expressed ⁠white supremacist ⁠views has been arrested on the day United States police believe he tried to attack a Hindu place of worship.

Police in the state of Illinois say they have thwarted a potential mass shooting and arrested Alexandros Paporakis, a Taco Bell cashier from the Chicago suburb of Palatine.

Prosecutors say he told colleagues he “couldn’t wait” to kill Indian people.

The case comes amid mounting concern among Indian Americans about hostility towards their community, fuelled by bitter political fights over immigration and skilled-worker visas.

So what do we know about the alleged plot, and is anti-Indian racism really on the rise in the US?

What happened?

Investigators say they believe Paporakis planned to attack the largest Hindu temple in Aurora, about 40 miles (65km) southwest of the Chicago suburb of Palatine in Illinois.

“However, the specific intended location has not been confirmed and remains under investigation,” police said.

Paporakis allegedly told colleagues that Sunday would be “a special day”.

According to prosecutors, a work colleague told investigators that Paporakis telephoned him on Sunday afternoon, saying his gun had jammed, ABC7 Chicago reported. He allegedly told his coworker he had left “super fast” without being seen.

He allegedly sent a video of the rifle failing to fire and said he wanted to try again once it was repaired, Fox 32 Chicago reported.

Two co-workers called police. Officers from Palatine and neighbouring Mount Prospect then arrested him as he left his home.

“The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated,” said Palatine Police Chief William Nord.

Paporakis faces felony charges of “making a terrorist threat” and “unlawful possession of a weapon”.

On Wednesday, a judge ordered him to be held in jail before a trial.

Prosecutors say Paporakis openly described himself to colleagues at work as a white supremacist.

He allegedly sent a co-worker an eight-page document titled, Why I fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto), according to a court document obtained by The Associated Press news agency.

It described Indian, Jewish and Black people as “subhumans” and set out a plan to kill as many of them as possible.

In it, he allegedly referred to himself as “a sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day”.

According to prosecutors, he wrote that he had been planning the attack for two years and had researched his target using YouTube and Google Street View, Fox 32 reported.

Prosecutors also said he had mental health issues and lived with his mother, according to ABC7.

A search of his home turned up an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines, a gas canister labelled with a slur aimed at South Asians and items bearing Nazi symbolism.

Is anti-Indian hate rising in the US?

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) does not count crimes against Indian Americans as a specific category. The closest measures are crimes against Hindus and Sikhs, most of whom in the US trace their roots to India.

Anti-Sikh crimes appear to be climbing. Police reported 234 anti-Sikh offences to the FBI in the 12 months to October, up from 183 in the previous 12 months, a rise of about 28 percent.

Anti-Hindu offences have remained lower and broadly steady, at 63 over the past two years, or two to three a month.

However, Hindu temples have been targeted.

Over two nights in late June 2025, an estimated 20 to 30 rounds were fired at a Krishna temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, while people were inside, according to the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. No one was hurt.

Two months later, Illinois Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi condemned a break-in and vandalism at a Hindu temple in Santa Clara, California, saying incidents targeting Hindu temples across the US “are on the rise”.

Online, the picture is starker.

A report by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH) found the monthly volume of hateful posts about South Asians on X more than tripled between January 2024 and June 2026.

Indian Americans say they are feeling it, too. A Carnegie Endowment for International Peace survey of 1,000 Indian Americans, conducted by YouGov between November 2025 and January 2026, found that one in four had been verbally abused with slurs since the start of 2025.

Nine percent said they had been physically threatened, and 4 percent physically assaulted.

Almost one in five said they had avoided wearing Indian dress in public.

Yet the survey also found no significant change in the number of people reporting personal discrimination since 2020.

Devesh Kapur, a professor of South Asian studies at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies and a co-author of the Carnegie survey, said the threat is growing.

“White supremacist extremism is clearly rising,” he told Al Jazeera. “Hostility towards Indians has particularly increased among the MAGA right in President Trump’s second term.”

What’s behind it?

Much of the hostility has been driven by fights over immigration, researchers say. Trump campaigned on the issue of immigration in the lead-up to the presidential election of 2024, and has launched sweeping restrictions on immigration – including “military-style” federal raids on immigrant communities, resulting in the deaths of some activists – since returning to the White House in January 2025.

Indians receive more than 70 percent of H-1B visas, which US employers use to bring skilled foreign workers to the country. Spikes in online hate have followed political rows over the programme.

In July 2025, President Donald Trump criticised US technology companies for outsourcing jobs to India. Days later, amid a trade dispute, he wrote on Truth Social that India and Russia could “take their dead economies down together”. That September, he imposed a $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B petitions. US courts are still deciding on the legality of the fee and have currently blocked the payment requirement.

Two-thirds of Indian Americans opposed the fee, the Carnegie survey found.

Figures close to Trump have also displayed anti-Indian attitudes. In September 2024, far-right activist Laura Loomer, at one time a close Trump ally, wrote that the White House would “smell like curry” if former Vice President Kamala Harris won the presidency. The White House, then under President Joe Biden, called the remark “repugnant”.

Kapur said Vice President JD Vance, whose wife is the daughter of Indian immigrants, had himself used “dog whistle” language, calling H-1B visa holders, most of them Indians, “indentured servants”. “It is therefore not surprising that such incendiary talk can spill over into violence,” Kapur said.

Government accounts have joined in, too. Last month, a since-deleted Department of Homeland Security post featured a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” and told him to “get off our roads”. The post came amid a Trump administration campaign to highlight the presence of undocumented immigrants in commercial trucking, particularly Sikhs and Indians.

Researchers also point to the growing prominence of South Asians in US politics, from Harris to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and to the “Great Replacement” conspiracy theory, which claims white populations are being deliberately replaced.

Paporakis is next due in court on October 30.

Police in the state of Illinois say they have thwarted a potential mass shooting and arrested Alexandros Paporakis, a Taco Bell cashier from the Chicago suburb of Palatine.

Prosecutors say he told colleagues he “couldn’t wait” to kill Indian people.

The case comes amid mounting concern among Indian Americans about hostility towards their community, fuelled by bitter political fights over immigration and skilled-worker visas.

So what do we know about the alleged plot, and is anti-Indian racism really on the rise in the US?

What happened?

Investigators say they believe Paporakis planned to attack the largest Hindu temple in Aurora, about 40 miles (65km) southwest of the Chicago suburb of Palatine in Illinois.

“However, the specific intended location has not been confirmed and remains under investigation,” police said.

Paporakis allegedly told colleagues that Sunday would be “a special day”.

According to prosecutors, a work colleague told investigators that Paporakis telephoned him on Sunday afternoon, saying his gun had jammed, ABC7 Chicago reported. He allegedly told his coworker he had left “super fast” without being seen.

He allegedly sent a video of the rifle failing to fire and said he wanted to try again once it was repaired, Fox 32 Chicago reported.

Two co-workers called police. Officers from Palatine and neighbouring Mount Prospect then arrested him as he left his home.

“The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated,” said Palatine Police Chief William Nord.

Paporakis faces felony charges of “making a terrorist threat” and “unlawful possession of a weapon”.

On Wednesday, a judge ordered him to be held in jail before a trial.

Prosecutors say Paporakis openly described himself to colleagues at work as a white supremacist.

He allegedly sent a co-worker an eight-page document titled, Why I fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto), according to a court document obtained by The Associated Press news agency.

It described Indian, Jewish and Black people as “subhumans” and set out a plan to kill as many of them as possible.

In it, he allegedly referred to himself as “a sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day”.

According to prosecutors, he wrote that he had been planning the attack for two years and had researched his target using YouTube and Google Street View, Fox 32 reported.

Prosecutors also said he had mental health issues and lived with his mother, according to ABC7.

A search of his home turned up an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines, a gas canister labelled with a slur aimed at South Asians and items bearing Nazi symbolism.

Is anti-Indian hate rising in the US?

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) does not count crimes against Indian Americans as a specific category. The closest measures are crimes against Hindus and Sikhs, most of whom in the US trace their roots to India.

Anti-Sikh crimes appear to be climbing. Police reported 234 anti-Sikh offences to the FBI in the 12 months to October, up from 183 in the previous 12 months, a rise of about 28 percent.

Anti-Hindu offences have remained lower and broadly steady, at 63 over the past two years, or two to three a month.

However, Hindu temples have been targeted.

Over two nights in late June 2025, an estimated 20 to 30 rounds were fired at a Krishna temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, while people were inside, according to the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. No one was hurt.

Two months later, Illinois Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi condemned a break-in and vandalism at a Hindu temple in Santa Clara, California, saying incidents targeting Hindu temples across the US “are on the rise”.

Online, the picture is starker.

A report by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH) found the monthly volume of hateful posts about South Asians on X more than tripled between January 2024 and June 2026.

Indian Americans say they are feeling it, too. A Carnegie Endowment for International Peace survey of 1,000 Indian Americans, conducted by YouGov between November 2025 and January 2026, found that one in four had been verbally abused with slurs since the start of 2025.

Nine percent said they had been physically threatened, and 4 percent physically assaulted.

Almost one in five said they had avoided wearing Indian dress in public.

Yet the survey also found no significant change in the number of people reporting personal discrimination since 2020.

Devesh Kapur, a professor of South Asian studies at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies and a co-author of the Carnegie survey, said the threat is growing.

“White supremacist extremism is clearly rising,” he told Al Jazeera. “Hostility towards Indians has particularly increased among the MAGA right in President Trump’s second term.”

What’s behind it?

Much of the hostility has been driven by fights over immigration, researchers say. Trump campaigned on the issue of immigration in the lead-up to the presidential election of 2024, and has launched sweeping restrictions on immigration – including “military-style” federal raids on immigrant communities, resulting in the deaths of some activists – since returning to the White House in January 2025.

Indians receive more than 70 percent of H-1B visas, which US employers use to bring skilled foreign workers to the country. Spikes in online hate have followed political rows over the programme.

In July 2025, President Donald Trump criticised US technology companies for outsourcing jobs to India. Days later, amid a trade dispute, he wrote on Truth Social that India and Russia could “take their dead economies down together”. That September, he imposed a $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B petitions. US courts are still deciding on the legality of the fee and have currently blocked the payment requirement.

Two-thirds of Indian Americans opposed the fee, the Carnegie survey found.

Figures close to Trump have also displayed anti-Indian attitudes. In September 2024, far-right activist Laura Loomer, at one time a close Trump ally, wrote that the White House would “smell like curry” if former Vice President Kamala Harris won the presidency. The White House, then under President Joe Biden, called the remark “repugnant”.

Kapur said Vice President JD Vance, whose wife is the daughter of Indian immigrants, had himself used “dog whistle” language, calling H-1B visa holders, most of them Indians, “indentured servants”. “It is therefore not surprising that such incendiary talk can spill over into violence,” Kapur said.

Government accounts have joined in, too. Last month, a since-deleted Department of Homeland Security post featured a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” and told him to “get off our roads”. The post came amid a Trump administration campaign to highlight the presence of undocumented immigrants in commercial trucking, particularly Sikhs and Indians.

Researchers also point to the growing prominence of South Asians in US politics, from Harris to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and to the “Great Replacement” conspiracy theory, which claims white populations are being deliberately replaced.

Paporakis is next due in court on October 30.
