news.title: Guns, F-bombs, fortune cookies. What do wild campaign ads actually say?
news.text:
Jennifer Balkcom, a Republican running for Congress in western North Carolina, introduced herself to voters by informing them that her single mom once shot a home intruder.

"You break into my house, you're going to get shot," Balkcom's mother says in her twangy mountain accent in a campaign ad posted Sept. 29 on YouTube, which already boasts over 800,000 views.

The camera then pans to Balkcom, a 48-year-old state representative, whose mom says she would bring her family's mountain toughness from their house to the House of Representatives as both women hold white coffee cups at a wooden dining room table.

The commercial is airing in one of the nation's most competitive congressional races and illustrates the metamorphosis of how campaign ads are produced and consumed during this midterm cycle.

Advertisements must be attention grabbing as both parties fight for visibility ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3, political experts, including Travis Ridout, a professor of government and public policy at Washington State University, say.

Can you sue over targeted ads? 'Blockbuster' Supreme Court case to decide

"I think just the capacity to target nowadays and tailor those messages to specific audiences means it's less (of) the standard generic ad that we're trying to appeal to all voters with," Ridout told USA TODAY.

Senator mired in controversy after skipping out on $700 cookie bill

Political spending during the 2025-26 election season has already surpassed $10 billion, exceeding the total ad spending in both the 2019-2020 and 2021-2022 election cycles, according to AdImpact Politics, an ad intelligence firm. AdImpact estimates that this year will mark the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history with upward to $11.6 billion in spending.

But it's not just the sheer size of the ad buys that stand out.

Candidates across the U.S. have used everything from F-bombs to fortune cookies to help boost their own prospects. Wisconsin state Rep. Steve Doyle even held a pet alpaca: "Please, don't fall for emotional appeals. Oh, and this is my baby alpaca, Pasta. She hopes you'll vote for me!" he joked.

Meanwhile, former President Barack Obama cut ads to support a slate of Democratic candidates while some Republicans are using their own spots to seek distance from President Donald Trump, who faces sinking approval ratings.

Viral F-bombs help flip fates in Illinois

In 2024, Cameron Shelton, a political science professor at Claremont McKenna College in California, found in his research that campaign ads confirm previously held biases.

"They're usually just sort of, 'How can I activate latent beliefs that somebody already has with very, very simple language and simple images?'" Shelton told USA TODAY.

Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton was struggling to break out from second place in February in an expensive, bitter Democratic primary to succeed Sen. Dick Durbin, the No. 2 to Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer.

Advisor Kaitlin Fahey, the CEO at Chicago-based Magnify Strategies political consulting firm, said Stratton had "one shot" to set herself apart from her opponents, Reps. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Robin Kelly.

The Senate races in reliably blue states like Illinois and nearby Minnesota may be sleepier than contests in Michigan or Texas, but the Democratic primaries were no less cutthroat.

Krishnamoorthi touted a massive war chest, including financial support from cryptocurrency PACs, while Kelly, a fellow Black woman, wielded the endorsement of the influential Congressional Black Caucus.

Then Stratton's "f Trump" ad went viral on X and helped her break out of the congested race.

Her Black dad couldn't go to Capitol. She could be a US senator

Trump's Midway Blitz immigration enforcement operations in Chicago had left a sour taste in the mouths of many Democratic primary voters – so Stratton's campaign released the profanity-laced spot in which several voters say "f--- Trump, vote Julianna" directly to the camera.

"They said it, not me," Stratton then quips, before pledging to stand up to the president.

The 30-second video ends with one last "f--- Trump" from Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth, and a final "vote Julianna" by Gov. JB Pritzker.

The Stratton apparatus knew the profanity-laced ad would make waves, and ruffle feathers, but it was ultimately successful, Fahey said.

"We also wanted to raise money off of it. We wanted to earn media attention," Fahey said of the viral video.

The ad garnered over 1.6 million all-time views on X. Fahey said her team also wanted the ad to shine more light on the safely blue race but noted that the campaign used other vehicles to discuss Stratton's core policy priorities.

While it's impossible to attribute a campaign's success to a single variable, Stratton went on to best Krishnamoorthi by seven points and Kelly by 22.

Political food fights

At least one Republican adopted a similar bold strategy. In July, Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tennessee, released a controversial ad when she faced an unexpectedly competitive field of primary opponents to replace Gov. Bill Lee.

The two-term senator's gubernatorial campaign video featured Blackburn at a Chinese restaurant, surrounded by bottles of soy sauce and fortune cookies wrapped in plastic packaging.

"How hard am I going to crack down on China?" Blackburn says, flanked by red booths. "Well, here's a clue." The 74-year-old lawmaker then smashed a series of fortune cookies over a menu while grimacing. A piece of fortune cookie paper read, "MARSHA BLACKBURN WILL FIGHT TO PROTECT TENNESSEE LAND FROM CHINA."

Blackburn won the Aug. 6 primary by 10 points over her closest challenger.

Swing-state candidates look for broad appeal

As candidates in red and blue races double down on appealing to their base, candidates in competitive general election races are aiming to show their independence.

Pennsylvania's first-term Rep. Rob Bresnahan is defending a seat he won by less than two points in 2024 in a race rated "toss-up" by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, which ranks political matchups across the country. (Balkcom, whose mom shot the intruder, faces Jamie Ager in a similar contest.)

He caught a bologna chub like a football in a new ad before slamming the meat log down on a kitchen island seemingly pulled straight out of ABC's 2000s suburban drama "Desperate Housewives."

"Paige Cognetti and her allies are full of baloney," Bresnahan says, referring to his Democratic opponent, the mayor of Joe Biden's hometown, Scranton. "Spending millions to paint me as something I am not."

In Iowa's toss-up Senate race, Rep. Ashley Hinson is creating space between herself and Trump – despite serving as a longtime surrogate – as she vies for the seat held by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst.

Ernst herself starred in a famous campaign commercial, "Squeal," in her first 2014 run for Senate in which she vowed to "make 'em squeal" after telling voters how she grew up castrating hogs.

In mid-September, Hinson's campaign released an ad featuring the congresswoman seated in a movie theater.

"It used to be that reaching across the aisle wasn't just OK, it was expected," Hinson says, as she handed over a bucket of popcorn across a theater aisle.

Monadnock Strategies founder Jesse Hunt, the former communications director at the Republican Governors Association, said campaigns target whatever group they need to win.

Democrat Josh Turek leads key Iowa Senate race, new poll shows

Sometimes, candidates woo base voters, Hunt said, and other times they seek support from independents like in Hinson's case.

"This might sound cliche, but it's all about what each campaign team believes is its winning coalition," Hunt said.

Hoops with Obama

Hinson's Democratic opponent, state Rep. Josh Turek, is running ads featuring Obama, who endorsed him in a basketball-themed July video. Obama, a noted basketball fan, shared his support for Turek, a two-time Paralympian in wheelchair basketball at the 2016 and 2020 Summer Games.

"Now, the ball's in your court," Obama says to Iowans.

Obama cut ads in October for a large slate of Democratic candidates in contentious races. He endorsed Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro for governor as well as Colorado's Phil Weiser, Wisconsin's David Crowley and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia who are competing in open gubernatorial contests.

He also endorsed Stratton, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Maine's Troy Jackson for Senate.

'I think most politicians are full of...'

In a swing district Trump won, one Democratic member of Congress is hoping to reuse unique tactics to distinguish her brand.

In 2024, Democratic state Sen. Kristen McDonald Rivet ran against Paul Junge in Michigan's 8th District, which became friendlier to Republicans after it was redrawn in 2023.

Now a congresswoman, Rivet enlisted the help of Declaration Media Group, a firm founded by Obama creative alumni who worked on successful battleground races in 2018 and 2020.

The Declaration team is again working with Rivet to win re-election in a district that includes Flint. The House member returned to a bar she filmed at during her first bid for Congress in a new ad.

"Two years ago, I sat right here and I told you this: 'I think most politicians are full of s---.' It's way worse than I thought," Rivet says.

"I approve this message because you deserve better than what you've been getting. I'm working hard to fix that," she adds while holding up a beer glass. A YouTube version posted Oct. 7 has nearly 1 million views.

Declaration consultants, including co-founder AJ Lenar, utilized Rivet's background in 2024 to separate her from national Democrats including then-President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost Michigan to Trump.

Last cycle, Lenar produced an ad where Rivet's husband threw himself out of a car. In the spot, the legislator obsesses over tax cuts on a neighborhood drive, so Joseph Rivet unbuckles his seatbelt and flings himself from the passenger seat of a red Chevrolet Impala.

"We knew that district was turning against us demographically, politically, right? And we just felt like we needed to do something that would make her stand out," Lenar told USA TODAY.

On Election Day, Rivet won by nearly 7 points while Trump prevailed over Harris by two percentage points in the district.

In an upcoming ad, Rivet's spouse will again reprise his role as sidekick – this time, Declaration applied special effects to set his hands on fire.

In the original bar spot, Declaration leaned into long held beliefs about sharing brews with officeholders.

"They say politics comes down to who you want to have a beer with, so here goes," Rivet says.

El-Sayed, Rogers clash: 4 takeaways from the Michigan Senate debate

Rivet, who used to run Michigan Head Start, also explains her biography: the lawmaker has six kids.

"I know, that's a lot," she says. "Now in the State Senate, I'm fighting to lower drug prices and housing costs and I helped pass the largest tax cut in state history."

"I root for the Lions, I hate Ohio and I think most politicians are full of s---," Rivet says. A beer glass slid into her right hand before she hoisted it up and said "Cheers!"

An ad standoff in Texas

Over 1,000 miles away from mid-Michigan, arguably no race has sparked more conversations about campaign advertising this cycle than the Texas Senate battle.

The Lone Star contest has been contentious since before the respective spring primaries determined Democratic state Rep. James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, would become their parties' nominees.

Talarico released an opening ad standing on a rusted pickup truck, surrounded by dozens of people in front of a church. "The biggest divide in our country is not left vs. right, it's top vs. bottom," the Presbyterian seminarian says to cheers.

Rep. Jasmine Crockett, a two-term Dallas area congresswoman who also competed in the primaries, shared an announcement video in which she stares to the side as audio of Trump insulting her plays.

The contrasting ads stoked online narratives about both candidates – one of which was that Talarico was a man of the people while Crockett was more self-serving. Crockett lost the Senate primary to Talarico, her pre-congressional colleague in the statehouse, in March.

Then Talarico's campaign produced several ads to underscore Paxton's ethical dilemmas after Paxton prevailed in a May primary runoff over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. In one August video, Talarico seized on Paxton taking a $1,000 Montblanc pen from a different man, lawyer Joe Joplin, in 2013 at the Collin County Courthouse.

The ad featured security footage ... and an endorsement from Joplin, the pen's owner.

Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, said Talarico's faith-based message has given his candidacy a distinctive identity. Talarico's campaign, Rottinghaus said, has cast him as a centrist who can appeal beyond the Democrats' national brand.

"He's able to present himself as somebody who's more moderate in a world that's very polarizing," Rottinghaus told USA TODAY.

Paxton is currently and very publicly estranged from his wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton. Recently, she starred in an early October ad that encouraged Republicans to vote red down the ticket.

Paxton's camp fought back, too. Their daughter, Mattie Hayworth Paxton, has appeared in multiple ads presenting her dad as a devoted father.

Texas is known for its uncertain terrain with its wetlands and deep canyons. The race's landscape is rough, too.

Rottinghaus said a win by Talarico could upend ideas about electability. He would be the first Texas Democrat to win a Senate seat since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.

But his videos won't matter as much as votes on Nov. 3.

Indians receive more than 70 percent of H-1B visas, which US employers use to bring skilled foreign workers to the country. Spikes in online hate have followed political rows over the programme.

In July 2025, President Donald Trump criticised US technology companies for outsourcing jobs to India. Days later, amid a trade dispute, he wrote on Truth Social that India and Russia could “take their dead economies down together”. That September, he imposed a $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B petitions. US courts are still deciding on the legality of the fee and have currently blocked the payment requirement.

Two-thirds of Indian Americans opposed the fee, the Carnegie survey found.

Figures close to Trump have also displayed anti-Indian attitudes. In September 2024, far-right activist Laura Loomer, at one time a close Trump ally, wrote that the White House would “smell like curry” if former Vice President Kamala Harris won the presidency. The White House, then under President Joe Biden, called the remark “repugnant”.

Kapur said Vice President JD Vance, whose wife is the daughter of Indian immigrants, had himself used “dog whistle” language, calling H-1B visa holders, most of them Indians, “indentured servants”. “It is therefore not surprising that such incendiary talk can spill over into violence,” Kapur said.

Government accounts have joined in, too. Last month, a since-deleted Department of Homeland Security post featured a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” and told him to “get off our roads”. The post came amid a Trump administration campaign to highlight the presence of undocumented immigrants in commercial trucking, particularly Sikhs and Indians.

Researchers also point to the growing prominence of South Asians in US politics, from Harris to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and to the “Great Replacement” conspiracy theory, which claims white populations are being deliberately replaced.

Paporakis is next due in court on October 30.
news.summary: Illinois teen who allegedly said he 'couldn’t wait' to kill Indians is arrested over a Hindu temple attack plot.

news.title: Ta-Nehisi Coates on the DSA, Mayor Mamdani, and Why Donald Trump Is the Dominant Figure of Our Age
news.text:
Ta-Nehisi is the author of multiple books, including We Were Eight Years in Power and Between the World and Me, which won a National Book Award in 2015.
Working with Ta-Nehisi is, honestly, one of the great privileges of my job, and we in the office look forward to getting his next column the way that some people look forward to Christmas.
In Ta-Nehisi’s latest for Vanity Fair, he turns his attention to President Trump, referring to him as a, quote, “visionary” politician. Someone who has seen and wielded his power to fundamentally alter the public perception of what an American president, or, indeed, any elected official, can do.
We talked not only about why Trump’s two presidencies are consequential, but also about the growing momentum around the Democratic Socialists of America just ahead of the midterms, why the way that Kamala Harris lost in 2024 matters, and how we begin to fix the damage that has been done.
Mark Guiducci: We’re here to talk about your new column that’s in the issue that’s just dropped, but I wanted to start with a question about yourself, which is that you’re sometimes referred to as a public intellectual. And I wanted to ask you about that term because—
Ta-Nehisi Coates: I fucking hate it.
Yeah, I thought you might. But tell me why. Just because it’s pretentious, or is there more to it?
Yeah, it’s just pretentious. Like, what do you do? What is your actual work? Like, what do you do? I mean, I’m a writer. I’m a writer and a journalist. It’s pretty easy to describe what I actually do. I like being identified with the actual work. I do not think of myself [as someone] who spends most of his working time just pontificating. Probably the thing that I love most about the job, even though it seems like I have these really strong opinions, is actually having the question before, putting the pieces together, talking to people, and trying to figure out what is actually going on. I’m rarely absolutely certain when I start anything. And if I am absolutely certain, it’s because I asked some questions a long time ago. And so that kind of interrogation, that kind of asking questions of the world, asking questions of yourself, quite frankly, is such an important part of the job. And rightly or wrongly, when I hear “public intellectual,” I think [of] some dude with a snifter and elbow patches kind of just sitting there, just dispensing his or her thoughts out into the world, and I don’t feel like that’s what I do.
No, I don’t think so. It’s almost like you’re a writer who thinks before they write.

That’s what I think it is. I also—
Wait, can you tell I don’t like being called a public intellectual? Could you tell?

Like, do I grimace?
We don’t even know each other that well, but I know you well enough to know that you would not like that. And so I was just curious to know, what would you prefer to be? Writer and journalist.
I think writer and journalist is just fine. I actually think it’s great honor in it too. There’s great honor in being a journalist. There’s great honor in being a writer. And so I enjoy it.
So in your latest column for Vanity Fair, about President Trump, you investigate how he has wielded his power in the second term. And in an interview with our own Aidan McLaughlin, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan talked about how Trump is the most consequential president of their lifetimes. But you go further than that. You talk about how he’s the most visionary politician of his era and the dominant American of our age. Tell me about what you meant by that.
You know, this started, actually, in his first term, and I was talking to my mother, who is not a Trump fan, but she said, “I feel his presence in my life constantly.” She never talked about any president, Republican or Democratic, in that way before. I think previously people and presidents in general, even when they’ve had a difficult relationship or a challenging relationship with the law, have kind of understood the law, customs, norms. It’s things that…I mean, maybe you step over them sometimes, maybe even break them sometimes, but you really shouldn’t. There’s a kind of caution in their brain. And he just has none of that.

He just has none of that. And I think what he’s really seen, rightly or wrongly—wrongly, obviously, from my political vantage point—is how much you can do, how much you can take. It never occurred to somebody that you could actually bend the American university system to your will. It never occurred to somebody that you could actually take opposing law firms that had worked for your opposition and not only get them, subject them to fines, but to actually have them actually work for you. Look, I think rightly or wrongly, and I’m saying it that way because I think even those of us who were not identified with his politics need to step back and take a second and look at what’s happened and look at the world we thought was possible and the world that actually is. When I was working at The Atlantic in 2016, one of the pieces I was most proud of I did was about President Obama, and we did this series of interviews in his Oval Office, and I’ll never forget him telling me Trump can’t win. Actually, he cannot win the presidency because Americans do not go for pessimism. Richard Nixon is an exception to that. In general, there has to be some sort of optimistic shame. You can’t come out here and do this thing about how bad we are and how awful everything is and how awful America is. And that turned out not just to be wrong about the election, but it turned out to be wrong about the era itself. And I don’t particularly hold Barack Obama responsible for that because I think a lot of people believed that. I think that was the dominant belief at the time, and he’s proved something different.
Maybe Trump himself believed that.
Yeah, because I don’t think he thought he was going to win.
Right. People say that his superpower is his absence of shame. But I think what you’re positing in your column is that there’s a creativity to it too. You call him visionary. He saw possibilities that none of us did, and you actually give him credit for that, which is something.
Yeah. No, I think you have to. I mean, people used to laugh at these lawsuits against these media and go, This is utterly ridiculous. There’s no way this is going to work.
Here we are.
Here we are.
So in the column, it’s quite sweeping in its approach, and you cover crypto and $TRUMP coin, his libertarian attitudes, his authoritarian attitudes, his diminution of the nation’s great law firms and universities you were mentioning, his bellicose foreign policy, his use of secret police and deportations. And finally, you start the column by… The lede is about the Great American Fair, which I wish... Our IP department probably disagrees, but I think would’ve been the perfect—you could have called that Vanity Fair, actually. But ultimately, nobody fights back is your point and that he’s getting away with it because perhaps everyone is still so stunned into submission. You actually write, “And to the extent that there is a genius to Donald Trump, it is in his apprehension of this reality, so very few people who matter care. When you’re the president, they let you do it.” What did you mean by that?
Oh man, that was very sad to write. It was very, very hard to write. I wrote that that way because there are people who do care. There are people who are fighting back. You certainly saw that in Minnesota. I mean, there are people who’ve died fighting back in this country. And so I don’t want to be dismissive of that. I think, Mark, what has most surprised me is people who would have told you about the greatness of American institutions, the greatness of American norms, the greatness of our legal system, the greatness of our university system, which is world-class, the greatness of the oldest democracy in the world—the very people who have benefited from that and who claimed credit for it were some of the first people who turned over, who rolled over, and weren’t willing to defend it. There was a lot of talk about the greatness and the importance of the press. Obviously, I’m a believer of that as a journalist, as I identified from the beginning, but the way in which we have just not fought for it has been, for me, a moment to question the extent to which certain people actually believed in it. And maybe that’s too harsh. Maybe more complicated is to say a heritage, a tradition, a legacy is not a thing that just kind of sits there and protects you. It has to be cared for. It has to be improved upon. And we speak a lot about our founding fathers, about our heritage, about our legacy, about our history, and maybe some of us got it in our head that these are not things that have to be fought for.
When I was in DC recently, I went to the [National] Portrait Gallery that houses all the portraits of the presidents all the way back. And there are brilliantly written captions, placards next to each portrait. I found that visit to be encouraging because we haven’t been here before, but we’ve been there before. Both in terms of how far we’ve strayed from the founding fathers, but also in terms of the power of the presidency, where do you place him?
I think that’s actually a great question. I think that’s a great question because I am probably the person that would have leaned toward, This actually is not new, that we actually do have a legacy of authoritarianism in this country. We have had a red scare before. We did have redemption after reconstruction before. We have seen our press not exactly always cover itself in glory. I think the thing that really, really distinguishes Trump is, we have not seen, first of all, just the level of profiteering. There is no record of somebody taking the Oval Office and then using it essentially to… I can’t remember how much money it is. I think, is it David Kirkpatrick at The New Yorker who’s doing that running tally? I think he’s up to $4 billion. That’s just never happened before.
Kara Swisher calls him the coin-operated president.
Right, right, right. And I don’t think that’s going to go away with him because there’s not going to be any sort of criminal trial. There’s not going to be any sort of repercussions at all. Why would someone not just assume, Oh, I can do this now. There’s nothing to stop me.
And not just the president, but every lawmaker.
Right. This was a taboo and now it’s not. I do think that’s actually different.
How do you restore taboo? How do you bring back shame?
You know what I think? I think it’s easier to destroy than it is to build. I think it’s going to take a lot. I think it’s going to take a lot. And so one of the reasons why I wrote that column in the way I did and with the aggression I did about calling him a visionary—insisting upon the level of his consequence is to say there really, really needs to be some serious, serious reflection about how you keep this from happening. Mark, honestly, that’s a very difficult question, because one would say, Okay, maybe we need new laws. But laws have to be enforced by people.
It’s cultural.

It’s cultural.
Right. And how do you do that?

How do you do that? If people don’t actually uphold norms, what do you do then? It’s actually a much, much thornier question, but I do think it merits some serious reflection.
He’s so deeply unpopular now.

And some people would say that we’ve seen him at his strongest and this war has changed things, and the midterms could reflect that. I wonder just how you feel about that unpopularity. Have people had enough?
Probably, but I don’t think people should take great comfort in that because the damage, for instance, done by the destruction of USAID, I mean, that just is what it is. Again, this column has forced me to give more credit than I want to to Donald Trump. But again, I do think he’s perceived and the movement behind him has perceived that you become popular in order to win the election and hold power, but you don’t necessarily hold power to become popular. Obviously, you need popularity to stay in power, but you hold power to do things. Ideally, you can do things and you can stay popular too, but they clearly do not care.

Actually doing the thing is clearly much, much more important to them. I wonder if there’s something to be said for that. And just so I’m absolutely clear about that, what is to be said is not that, with my politics, that you need a left-wing version of this, right? That we shouldn’t care about norms, that we shouldn’t care, that we need somebody that’s going to go in there and profiteer. That’s not what I’m getting at, but I do think perhaps there is another version, a more healthier version, of imagination that could be exercised.
How do you see this ending? Because some would say that even if he’s not in office, that he will remain this dominant American figure, and I’m curious to know what ways out you see.
The presidency, particularly in the post–World War II era, it’s a very, very powerful position. Even presidents who people view their terms as failures, their ghosts linger. I don’t know if, for instance, the Democratic Party has ever gotten over how it perceived Carter as president. I don’t know that that’s gone away. Certainly Nixon is still with us.
To say nothing of Reagan.
To say nothing of Reagan. To say nothing of ones that people actually view as successful. And so I think this one’s going to leave a mark, man.

I think it’s gonna leave a mark. I think it has said some things are possible for some very, very dark forces in this country. I need to add that we also need to have some humility and some reflection about the fact that in other countries and in other democracies, people don’t always respond the way that we’ve responded. Brazil had an attempted coup also, and they didn’t respond the way we did. South Korea, they didn’t respond the way we did. And so I think there’s some—
You mean by reelecting him?
Yeah. And by effectively immunizing and saying, Yeah, you can run again. Go, go, go. It’s fine. There was clearly some sense that, no, there needs to be some consequence here. I think we need to ask ourselves why. Why did we not do that? And actually, I think that relates back to your question about popularity. Look, Americans are working jobs, trying to keep their heads above water. They can’t keep up with every little thing that’s happening. And if there’s ire in this column, it is for the elite class of Americans, and I don’t mean that in a derogatory way. I mean that in the most literal way. The caretakers of American democracy, I think they failed here. I guess I include myself as a journalist. I think we failed here, because I’m a journalist, right? I’m part of it. I think we failed here, and everybody’s elite, everybody’s caretakers of the state don’t respond this way. It’s not like, Oh, this is just what happens. No, this is ours. So what does that say about us?
Even on Epstein, when you think about Epstein in the way that the British have responded, you’re out.
Yeah. Yeah.
It doesn’t matter if you’re royal, you’re out. And I think that that is a worthwhile example. There are rules and things that you… Anyway.
No, but you’re onto something. There’s a great book by Chris Hayes. It’s from 2012. He’s obviously gone on to become this incredible journalist, but before he became Chris Hayes as we know him now, he wrote this book, Twilight of the Elites, that I just think was prophetic and predictive. And it’s a pretty wide-ranging book because it goes from Major League Baseball to the Catholic Church to the political system. And what it says is there is a failure in the governance of elite institutions across the board. It’s actually deeply, deeply problematic for the country. And that book bore out to be exactly right.
It had already corroded that many years before.
Yeah. I mean, he was saying this in Obama’s first term. He was saying, Listen, we’ve got a real, real problem. And you can see it here. You can see it now.
Yeah. The DSA has incredible momentum, but I’m curious about, within the DSAs—it’s a fractured organization, but within the national chapter’s manifesto, there’s a—
A lot of interesting stuff.
A lot of interesting stuff. There’s a call to abolish the presidency, abolish the Senate. And you were saying earlier, it’s a lot easier to destroy than it is to build. I’m curious just where your head is at.
My head is at, I want to write about the DSA for Vanity Fair.

That’s where my head… I have many, many questions.
We agree on that.
No, I have many, many questions, and some of them... Okay, this is beautiful because I’ll just speak about where I’m at right now, and then you can see the thing in motion.
Okay, cool.
I don’t quite understand what the DSA is, and I don’t mean that in a derogatory way.
No, me either.
I mean, if I had to point out, Okay, there’s that governance structure; this is where Zohran Mamdani stands, this is where the national chapter stands, this is where this person, this is how this happened—I couldn’t do that for you. I couldn’t actually do that for you right now. And I’ll be honest, I have not quite read the piece of journalism that’s actually done it for me, that’s made me understand this movement. I’m putting value judgments aside, whatever you think of it, you know what I mean?

What is actually going on here? And I guess this is my frustration.
Because it’s powerful.
It is. It is. It is. I mean, clearly, right? And so my frustration with journalism at this moment is there has been too much, What does this mean for the midterms? What does this mean for the Democratic Party? And not enough, Okay, but what is this? How’d this happen?
What is this?
You know what I mean? If I read another scene from a DSA party in Brooklyn where people are drinking beer and doing whatever, I’m going to scream. I don’t care about how they socialize. I want to know what they’re doing. What are they?
Yeah. Enough scene reports, enough trend reports.
Enough, enough. Give me the nitty-gritty. You know what I mean?

So this is where I start. This is why I don’t want to be called a public intellectual, to go all the way back. Obviously, I have some politics and some thoughts about all this, but at my root, I go to bed thinking, What is going on?
It’s curiosity.

I also want to ask you about your column in our summer issue about Vice President Harris and her run for the presidency, that perhaps the fatal flaw of her campaign was her inability to acknowledge what was happening in Palestine and perhaps the inappropriate use of Black women civil rights leaders in that campaign.
Yeah. I mean, I don’t know that that would’ve won her the presidency. So again, this starts with Vanity Fair, quite honestly. I was sent out in 2024 for Vanity Fair to cover the DNC. It was kind of a broad sort of mandate, which was sort of cool because we didn’t know what we were going to see. You don’t know what's actually going to happen. So I go out there and what I see is this relatively small Uncommitted Movement, which at that point was demanding that either there’d be a Palestinian American speaker or an Arab American speaker. There had not been an Arab American speaker at the DNC since 1988.
They were asking for a lot of other things besides that, but that was the big thing, right? And then they would use that to go back to their communities and say, Okay, this is somebody we can actually support. Two things happened. The first thing was there were a lot of normie Dems who had never heard of the Uncommitted Movement, who I would just watch from afar, and they would come up to these guys. There was a lot of energy around it. They wanted to know what was going on. What is this? Who are you? Actually, it was not as fractious up close as it ultimately looked to be. It was actually quite a bit of curiosity. And the second thing that happened was, obviously, they were unsuccessful. I have never run a campaign. I’m not what you would call a political strategist in any respect. I do think that people in life should think about how they want to lose, though. I do think that’s an actual clarifying exercise. And I do think—
Explain that.
Yeah. I mean, I do it in my own life. Just personally, I do it, because it gives you an idea of, what are your boundaries? Where’s the thing, like, No, no, no, it’s not worth it? No, I don’t want it. You know what I mean? Actually, if I have to give it up this way, then that’s fine. I’m okay. I can sleep at night.
Where’s the tap-out moment?
Where’s the tap-out moment? Exactly.

And I do think losing because, especially given how the issue has moved, losing because Kamala Harris said in public what numerous people said to me, in my reporting, she said in private, I think that would be viewed very differently today. And I think the party would view her very, very differently today. I do think that matters. I think how she lost actually mattered. And I say that to say, maybe she would’ve lost anyway. Maybe she allows a Palestinian American speaker up there. She still loses. Maybe she says, “What is happening in Gaza right now is unacceptable and under my presidency, I will enforce the Leahy Law,” which is to say we will be looking at human rights abuses and linking that to our armed shipment. Maybe she loses anyway. Maybe that is the case, but there’s a difference between being seen as somebody who did not have the courage of your convictions and being seen as prophetic.
In that column, you suggest, posit even, that the presidency is an office maybe antithetical to the kinds of values that—
That elevate Black politicians there in the first place.
That elevate Black politicians there in the first place. But I’m going to try to end this on a positive note.
Yes. I thought I ended that piece on a positive note.
You did, you did. But the kind of vision that Donald Trump has clearly been able to have about what the presidency is, is perhaps what would be needed for someone, her or otherwise, to put those pieces together.
You know what I think is needed is… The lesson to take from this is, under previous presidents, it was always, Look, this is as far as it goes. This is what this thing is. This is what was inherited to me. This is what it is. This is what it’ll be. I think what Trump has shown is there can be considerable imagination about what that thing actually is. And you don’t have to root your imagination in the darkest fears, the rage, in the resentments of Americans. You can perhaps root them somewhere else. Just to go back to your DSA question, I think you’re kind of seeing that with Zohran.

I don’t think people thought about the mayor’s office like this. Like, what? I should be looking at social media and seeing who’s mad about a pothole, and then I should fill it and that could be a thing? People actually care about that? I don’t think anybody thought of that.
No, he’s a reflection of imagination, both his own and that of the city that was able to see this happen.
Yes, yes, yes. And I think you’re going to need some of that. I think you’re going to need some of that to close that gap that I was talking about in the article.
Yeah. Well, I look forward to the column about the DSA then.
I look forward to it too. Can’t wait.
Okay. Ta-Nehisi, thanks for coming.
Thanks, Mark. Thanks so much.
About Fair Game
Fair Game is Vanity Fair’s flagship interview show, where nothing is off-limits. Editor Mark Guiducci hosts in-depth and far-reaching conversations with the most interesting characters from the worlds of Hollywood, politics, style, Silicon Valley, and beyond. It’s all Fair Game.
news.summary: In a wide-ranging conversation with Mark Guiducci, Coates discusses his latest column for Vanity Fair and why Trump is “the most visionary politician of his era.”

news.title: Kamala Harris criticizes Biden administration's failure to curb Israel's conduct during Gaza war
news.text: Former US vice president Kamala Harris criticized former US president Joe Biden's administration's response to Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza during the 2026 Asan Memorial Lecture in Seoul on Wednesday.Harris said that the United States needed to uphold its obligation to international law and that the Biden administration's response to Israel's war was a failure in that regard.The former vice president called out the "failure to use our leverage to curtail the Israeli government's horrific conduct in the war in Gaza," saying that the Biden administration should have acted "sooner and more fully."Harris also criticized the current US government under US President Donald Trump, saying that it "offers Netanyahu a blank check."She also discussed the modern development of American foreign policy, saying that the "orthodoxies of old" were insufficient for current challenges.“Coming out of world wars, and into the Cold War, military might was the primary source of power,” she said. “But now more than ever, economic innovation, markets and minerals, chips and computers, have greater influence.”Kamala Harris plays coy on 2028 presidential runShe also said US relations and alliances must be strengthened. “The growing relationship between, for example, China and Russia and Iran and North Korea is something we have to pay attention to, and it should be the reason that within our alliance that we are committed to strengthening what must, without any question, happen in terms of deterrence," she said.Harris also expressed confidence that Democrats will win the upcoming US midterm election, though she avoided directly answering whether she was considering a 2028 presidential run. "2028, from my perspective, doesn't matter if we don't win 2026."

news.title: Weapons of Mass Division
news.text:
There’s a growing movement called Blue Dot Farmers, supposedly a coalition connecting consumers with farmers and ranchers who share their values.

The idea is to buy beef, dairy, eggs, and produce from farmers whose beliefs align with yours. On the surface, connecting consumers with independent farmers sounds like something I could get behind.

But apparently, the values we’re talking about aren’t necessarily how you treat your animals, whether you’re rebuilding soil, or what chemicals you use. They’re increasingly about who you voted for.

Matt, a social media personality known as Necessary Noise, launched a Blue Dot Farmers Facebook group that has grown to approximately 49,000 members. The movement recently received international attention in a Times article titled “The beef battleground: Americans boycott food from Trump-voting farmers.”

Matt has been making videos confronting farmers who voted for Donald Trump and are now struggling financially or frustrated with agricultural policies. Rather than offering compassion to people whose livelihoods are already under pressure, he publicly shames them for their votes. He told The Times those farmers had made their own bed.

I’ve experienced a version of this myself.

Recently, I posted an Instagram video standing in my pasture, cowboy hat on, cows behind me, talking about imported beef and what it means for the American cattle industry. I wasn’t asking anyone to feel sorry for me. I was talking about an industry I’m part of and arguing that Americans should support American farmers and ranchers.

That video received 699 comments on Instagram alone. Many weren’t discussing imported beef or cattle prices. They were discussing who I voted for.

Somehow a conversation about the American cattle industry had become a referendum on my presidential vote.

My brother, Ryland Engelhart, co-founded Kiss the Ground and has spent years bringing regenerative agriculture to unlikely audiences. Recently, we attended a dinner connected to Congressman Chip Roy’s office. The next morning, he flew to New York for Climate Week and attended a luncheon with Governor Gavin Newsom and his wife.

I believe California’s policies destroyed my businesses and much of my life’s work. But Ryland understands that changing things means sitting with people you profoundly disagree with. That’s bridge-building.

I voted for Trump. I also voted for Barack Obama.

I joke that I’m politically nonbinary. I believe in God. I’m an environmentalist, pro-life, pro-family, antiwar, and a believer in the Constitution. I believe you cannot be born in the wrong body. My husband was illegal when we married, or undocumented, depending on whether you’re a blue dot or a red dot. I think adults should be free to buy meat and dairy directly from one another without government permission.

So which box am I supposed to fit into?

I don’t regret voting for Trump. I don’t agree with everything he does, but nothing I saw from Kamala Harris during her vice presidency convinced me she would have been better for farmers. We cannot know how an administration that never existed would have governed.

Voting isn’t a lifelong pledge to defend every decision that follows. I don’t even agree with everything my husband does, and we’re married and raising children together.

I watched government decisions during COVID-19 devastate businesses, including mine. Restrictions began under Trump but were imposed largely by state and local governments and lasted longer in many Democratic-led states, including California. I watched restaurants close and children struggle through prolonged school closures.

I could spend my days shaming Biden voters for policies imposed by politicians they supported. I don’t. They made decisions for their own reasons, just as I did.

My neighbor Chuck taught me something about political labels. Years ago, while I still lived in California but owned the ranch next to his, he called after seeing me on Fox News.

“Girl, I about choked when I saw my Democratic neighbor on Fox News! Why’d they hire you?”

He assumed that California, or my husband, meant we were on different teams. But Chuck and I voted for the same president.

We share a vote but disagree profoundly about farming. Are our values aligned?

Now, imagine I’m a Democrat buying beef from a politically aligned farmer. Who did his hay grower vote for? His mechanic? His feed supplier? The neighbor who loaned him a tractor? The trucker? The meat processor?

How far must I follow my dollar before I’m sure it hasn’t reached a Republican?

I encountered this thinking when I owned organic vegan restaurants. People asked whether I bought produce from vegan farms. But organic agriculture often relies on animal agriculture. Farmers use manure, bone meal, blood meal, and other animal-derived fertilizers. Growing organically without animal inputs is possible, but finding a reliable commercial supply grown entirely without them was another matter.

The vegetables on a vegan plate may have been nourished by cows or chickens. Food systems are tangled together. Life feeds on life.

And was every cook vegan? Every dishwasher or delivery driver? I spent hundreds of thousands on payroll. Was I supposed to police where employees spent their wages?

Money refuses to stay inside ideological fences.

I believe in voting with our dollars. But I want consumers voting for farming practices. Is the farmer rebuilding soil? Reducing chemicals? Protecting water? Treating animals well?

Several websites using the Blue Dot name describe agricultural ideals, but I couldn’t confirm that Matt runs or is affiliated with them. What has been documented about his Facebook group is political vetting. I couldn’t find comparable evidence of checks on soil health, chemical use, or livestock practices.

What makes a farmer a blue dot? The way they farm or the way they vote?

Matt and I probably agree about plenty. Chuck and I voted alike but disagree profoundly about farming. People who vote differently can share values. People who vote alike can share almost nothing else.

There will always be another election, another administration, another swing in a different direction. But farmers will still need to grow food, ranchers will still need to care for their animals, and neighbors will still need one another.

Healthy soil requires diversity. Beneath our feet, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, and countless other organisms perform different functions and exchange nutrients. Resilient soil isn’t created by making every organism identical. It is built through diversity and relationships.

I believe healthy communities work the same way. We don’t need everyone to think alike, vote alike, worship alike, or agree about every issue.

Long after the election signs come down, we’re still going to be neighbors. We’re still going to need each other.

Who are we going to be for one another?

My values align with humanity.

There’s a growing movement called Blue Dot Farmers, supposedly a coalition connecting consumers with farmers and ranchers who share their values.

The idea is to buy beef, dairy, eggs, and produce from farmers whose beliefs align with yours. On the surface, connecting consumers with independent farmers sounds like something I could get behind.

But apparently, the values we’re talking about aren’t necessarily how you treat your animals, whether you’re rebuilding soil, or what chemicals you use. They’re increasingly about who you voted for.

Matt, a social media personality known as Necessary Noise, launched a Blue Dot Farmers Facebook group that has grown to approximately 49,000 members. The movement recently received international attention in a Times article titled “The beef battleground: Americans boycott food from Trump-voting farmers.”

Matt has been making videos confronting farmers who voted for Donald Trump and are now struggling financially or frustrated with agricultural policies. Rather than offering compassion to people whose livelihoods are already under pressure, he publicly shames them for their votes. He told The Times those farmers had made their own bed.

I’ve experienced a version of this myself.

Recently, I posted an Instagram video standing in my pasture, cowboy hat on, cows behind me, talking about imported beef and what it means for the American cattle industry. I wasn’t asking anyone to feel sorry for me. I was talking about an industry I’m part of and arguing that Americans should support American farmers and ranchers.

That video received 699 comments on Instagram alone. Many weren’t discussing imported beef or cattle prices. They were discussing who I voted for.

Somehow a conversation about the American cattle industry had become a referendum on my presidential vote.

My brother, Ryland Engelhart, co-founded Kiss the Ground and has spent years bringing regenerative agriculture to unlikely audiences. Recently, we attended a dinner connected to Congressman Chip Roy’s office. The next morning, he flew to New York for Climate Week and attended a luncheon with Governor Gavin Newsom and his wife.

I believe California’s policies destroyed my businesses and much of my life’s work. But Ryland understands that changing things means sitting with people you profoundly disagree with. That’s bridge-building.

I voted for Trump. I also voted for Barack Obama.

I joke that I’m politically nonbinary. I believe in God. I’m an environmentalist, pro-life, pro-family, antiwar, and a believer in the Constitution. I believe you cannot be born in the wrong body. My husband was illegal when we married, or undocumented, depending on whether you’re a blue dot or a red dot. I think adults should be free to buy meat and dairy directly from one another without government permission.

So which box am I supposed to fit into?

I don’t regret voting for Trump. I don’t agree with everything he does, but nothing I saw from Kamala Harris during her vice presidency convinced me she would have been better for farmers. We cannot know how an administration that never existed would have governed.

Voting isn’t a lifelong pledge to defend every decision that follows. I don’t even agree with everything my husband does, and we’re married and raising children together.

I watched government decisions during COVID-19 devastate businesses, including mine. Restrictions began under Trump but were imposed largely by state and local governments and lasted longer in many Democratic-led states, including California. I watched restaurants close and children struggle through prolonged school closures.

I could spend my days shaming Biden voters for policies imposed by politicians they supported. I don’t. They made decisions for their own reasons, just as I did.

My neighbor Chuck taught me something about political labels. Years ago, while I still lived in California but owned the ranch next to his, he called after seeing me on Fox News.

He assumed that California, or my husband, meant we were on different teams. But Chuck and I voted for the same president.

We share a vote but disagree profoundly about farming. Are our values aligned?

How far must I follow my dollar before I’m sure it hasn’t reached a Republican?

I encountered this thinking when I owned organic vegan restaurants. People asked whether I bought produce from vegan farms. But organic agriculture often relies on animal agriculture. Farmers use manure, bone meal, blood meal, and other animal-derived fertilizers. Growing organically without animal inputs is possible, but finding a reliable commercial supply grown entirely without them was another matter.

The vegetables on a vegan plate may have been nourished by cows or chickens. Food systems are tangled together. Life feeds on life.

And was every cook vegan? Every dishwasher or delivery driver? I spent hundreds of thousands on payroll. Was I supposed to police where employees spent their wages?

Money refuses to stay inside ideological fences.

I believe in voting with our dollars. But I want consumers voting for farming practices. Is the farmer rebuilding soil? Reducing chemicals? Protecting water? Treating animals well?

news.title: Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business
news.text:
Serbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal.

Aleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office.

The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’ global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates.

The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption.

A nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s son Donald Trump Jr and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios.

After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučić threatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”.

“We have lost an exceptional investment,” the Serbian president said. “I will personally ensure that everyone who participated in causing this damage is held accountable.”

Vučić’s culture minister is among those charged with abuse of power. But a Guardian investigation, drawing on interviews and leaked documents, reveals that the Serbian president himself led the initial meeting where the alleged scheme was discussed. This crucial meeting is not mentioned in the indictment, raising questions about what information the prosecutors are holding back and why.

Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner said they had no part in the removal of the building’s protected status and that it would be “false” to say the Belgrade project was part of a “pay to play” scheme.

Vučić did not respond to requests for comment. His decision to call a snap election means that a hearing at which witnesses might reveal details of his involvement will not take place until after the vote.

A free 99-year lease

On 6 February 2024, Dubravka Đukanović, a Serbian conservation professor in her 60s, arrived for a meeting at the presidency, a domed former royal palace. For three years, she had been the director of the country’s institute for the protection of cultural monuments.

The topic was the General Staff building, the former Yugoslav ministry of defence in central Belgrade. The building, an architectural gem seen as an emblem of resistance to the Nazis, was already cherished when Nato forces bombed it in 1999 during its campaign to force Milošević to withdraw from Kosovo, deepening its resonance.

Vučić himself had reaffirmed the General Staff building’s legally protected status in 2016. Now, the president said he wanted Đukanović to rescind it, according to two people with knowledge of the meeting. Some unspecified “foreign investor” was keen on the site.

Under Serbian law, stripping the General Staff building of its protected status was not in Đukanović’s gift. Her institute would have to commission an expert opinion, which would have to conclude that there were good reasons why protected status was no longer merited.

But the president wanted it done. At 6ft 6in and intolerant of dissent, Vučić can be intimidating. His tone towards Đukanović and another heritage official present was unpleasant, the sources said. He told them they were lazy and incompetent. The message was clear: do what I want or resign.

A plausible explanation for Vučić’s forceful intervention came the following month, when an agreement between the Serbian government and Kushner’s real estate company leaked.

Married to Trump’s daughter Ivanka, Kushner had been an influential White House aide during his father-in-law’s first term. Since Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election, Kushner had been concentrating on his investment fund.

By early 2024, Trump was storming to the Republican nomination and was favourite to win the coming election. If Trump took back the White House, Kushner would once more be one of the most influential people on the planet.

The leaked agreement showed the Serbian authorities had granted Kushner’s company a 99-year lease over the General Staff site, free of charge.

Kushner, whose spokesperson said he had been looking at the project since 2021, posted an image of the design on X, professing himself “excited”.

The news was not universally welcomed in Belgrade. “Serbia is not a buffet, and Vučić is not a waiter,” said Aleksandar Jovanović Ćuta, an environmental activist who revealed the agreement. “This is not his private property.”

Yet Vučić’s regime proceeded to sign a contract, dated 13 May 2024 and seen by the Guardian, undertaking that the “cultural heritage designation” of the site would be removed “to the satisfaction” of Kushner’s company.

Comply or resign

The week after the contract was signed, Đukanović was summoned to another meeting. The president was not there this time. Siniša Mali, his finance minister and right-hand man, took charge.

Mali urged Đukanović and Olivera Vučković, Belgrade’s top heritage official, to cancel the General Staff site’s protected status, according to the indictment’s summary of testimony the two women would later give prosecutors. It makes no reference to the earlier meeting with the president but indicates that the subject had previously been broached.

“Mali asked them if they had given it any thought,” the indictment says, “and if they would initiate the procedure to remove the building’s protected status.”

The women refused, “believing that the legal conditions for it were not met”. In that case, Mali told them, repeating his boss’s ultimatum from February, they should resign. They did.

In her resignation letter, which the Guardian has seen, Đukanović wrote that she could not agree “to inappropriate interventions that would permanently destroy all the values of the complex, which testifies to the highest achievements of contemporary Serbian architecture and is of incalculable importance for preserving enduring creative values, the education of future generations, and the strengthening of the cultural identity of the Serbian people”.

Approached by the Guardian, Đukanović and Vučković confirmed the accuracy of this account. Đukanović added: “I prefer not to make any statement on this matter while the court proceedings are ongoing.”

Little was heard of the General Staff plan for months. In November, Trump beat Kamala Harris to win re-election. Ten days later, Vučić’s government announced that the General Staff site had been stripped of its protected status.

Keeping it in the family

One of the first things Trump did upon regaining the presidency was to ditch the pledge he made in his first term that his family business would refrain from doing deals abroad while he was in office.

“The scale of corruption will be orders of magnitude greater than what we saw in the first Trump administration,” Kathleen Clark, a government ethics lawyer at Washington University School of Law, warned at the time. Trump had made it much easier, she said, to buy his favour.

The family business remained officially under the control of his two oldest sons, Don Jr and Eric. In January 2025, four days after their father’s inauguration, Eric spoke about some new projects. The Trumps and the Kushners, New York real estate families united by marriage, had decided to embark on their first venture together: Kushner’s Belgrade hotel and tower would bear the Trump name.

“It’s going to be fun to bring the family together,” Eric told the New York Times. “Serbia is one of the fastest-growing countries in Europe, and we’re incredibly honoured to be there.” Kushner, who had travelled to Belgrade for what Vučić called an “inspiring” meeting with the Serbian leader, added: “Our research showed that the Trump brand would be the best for this market.”

That brand has enjoyed a surge in demand around the world during Trump’s second term, accompanied by allegations that it comes with a quid pro quo.

In Vietnam, Eric was showered with confetti at the groundbreaking ceremony for a £1.5bn golf resort, the permits for which were granted with unusual speed. Then Trump halved Vietnam’s tariffs. The Saudis poured money into Kushner’s fund, and plans emerged for a Trump plaza in Jeddah. Then Trump agreed to sell the kingdom new US fighter jets. A cryptocurrency baron’s company and senior Emiratis cut a lucrative transaction with World Liberty Financial, the digital currency venture Don Jr and Eric founded. Trump gave the crypto baron a pardon and the Emiratis access to restricted US chips.

Asked about such deals last year, Kushner, now a presidential envoy to Russia, Israel and elsewhere, said: “What people call conflicts of interests … I call experience and trusted relationships that we have throughout the world.”

Those who strike up “trusted relationships” with the Trumps, even if there is not an obvious quid pro quo, gain something less tangible but maybe still more valuable: the aura of friendship with a president who is happy to wield his superpower to make or break smaller nations and their leaders.

Vučić has plenty in common with Trump. Both are friendly with Vladimir Putin and contemptuous of the EU – in Vučić’s case, despite his country having applied to join. A shared disdain for Nato may help explain why the one part of the General Staff building’s heritage that the redevelopment pledged to retain was a memorial to the alliance’s “aggression” against Serbia.

And there is a lot that Vučić could use US help with, not least the fate of Kosovo, which he says is still part of Serbia.

Not long after his father returned to office, Don Jr landed in Belgrade. Vučić said that during their meeting he “emphasised the importance of the economic and political relations between Serbia and the USA and stressed the importance of strategic cooperation between the two countries and joint projects in the years to come”. When Don Jr returned the following month, Vučić fed him a choice sucking-pig.

For Vučić, the support of the first family was timely. Days before his regime stripped the General Staff site of its protection, the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people, triggered rolling protests against graft. The student organisers’ slogan has become “Serbia or mafia”.

Don Jr’s visit came on the eve of the biggest demonstration in Serbia’s history. He invited Vučić on to his podcast, Triggered, and declared that the Serb ruler’s opponents were “weaponising” the Novi Sad disaster, just as Trump’s had done with the Capitol riots after his 2020 election defeat.

But the protesters maintained their momentum, and began to rally against the Trump tower. In May 2025, Vučić went to the US, hoping to visit Trump at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida members’ club. He got to see Rudy Giuliani, Trump’s disgraced lawyer, but not the president. State media reported this was because Vučić fell ill.

No sooner was Vučić home than police arrested Goran Vasić, the man who had been installed as head of the heritage institute to replace Dubravka Đukanović following her resignation. To achieve the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protected status, prosecutors said, Vasic had forged a supportive expert opinion.

More arrests followed. In December 2025, Vučić’s culture minister was indicted for abuse of office for his alleged part in the General Staff scheme. Within days, Kushner’s company announced the project was off.

Coup or cover-up?

Vučić’s threat of reprisals was not idle.

His allies attacked Đukanović, claiming that she had tried to profit personally from her time as a heritage official. Her deputy, who received a visit from the state security service after she went on television to denounce the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protection, has been accused of unrelated misconduct. The Serbian conservators’ industry body said this had “the obvious aim of discrediting her”. Both are expected to give evidence in the criminal proceedings.

For the specialist unit of organised-crime prosecutors who brought the charges, this is a watershed case. Never before has a serving Serbian minister been indicted.

Vučić accuses the prosecutors of staging a coup. Others, though, fear they are pulling their punches. That concern increased when Nikola Selaković, the indicted culture minister, used a court appearance in April to reveal that, while police were raiding his ministry, he was in his office sipping plum brandy and smoking cigarettes with Mladen Nenadić, the head of the organised-crime prosecutors’ unit. The unit’s spokesperson said there was “no discussion regarding the course of the case”.

“In everything that happened regarding potential investments, I saw a chance for our country and citizens,” said Selaković, who faces three years in prison if convicted.

Vučić has not been charged. Neither has his lieutenant, Mali. Both deny wrongdoing.

The indictment refers to evidence from witnesses who were present at the Vučić meeting in February 2024 but does not mention it, raising questions about the apparent decision to omit what would appear to be a key part of the narrative.

The spokesperson for the organised crime prosecutors’ unit said that it had evidence regarding Vučić’s February 2024 meeting with the heritage officials. Beyond those already indicted, prosecutors were “conducting pretrial proceedings in this case to determine potential criminal liability of other persons as well”, the spokesperson added.

Vučić has stepped down and cannot seek another term but is expected to retain his control over the regime if he is elected prime minister on 25 October. In one of his last acts as president, he issued 49 pardons. Some of the recipients have not been identified and it is not clear whether they include defendants in the General Staff case.

The White House referred questions to the Trumps’ company. Its representative said: “The Trump Organization has no plans to develop any project in Belgrade, was never, at any point, involved in any discussions or negotiations to acquire any site in Belgrade and denies any involvement in or knowledge of the alleged claims.”

Kushner’s spokesperson said: “The suggestion that Jared Kushner pursued the Belgrade project as part of any political arrangement or ‘pay to play’ scheme is categorically false.” Rather, it was “an opportunity to transform a site associated with a painful chapter in Serbia’s history into a symbol of healing and reconciliation, while bringing substantial private investment, jobs and economic opportunity to Belgrade”.

The spokesperson added: “Jared had no involvement in the Serbian government’s internal processes concerning the site’s protected status.”

For all Vučić’s difficulties, the tale of the Trump Tower Belgrade does not appear to have put others off doing business with the first family. Trump retains stakes in dozens of his companies, even if his sons nominally run them. In July, he released his financial disclosure for his first year back at the White House. It showed he had made $2bn.

news.title: Woke megachurch pastor, Dem nominee called for repentance over White privilege in wake of George Floyd, BLM
news.text: A former pastor and candidate running to make history in deep-red Kansas once suggested that people should repent for their White privilege as protests against the death of George Floyd rippled through the country. During the tumultuous summer of 2020, just days after Floyd’s killing in Minnesota, Adam Hamilton called on his congregation at the Church of the Resurrection to recognize their White privilege and repent. "Like part of what I know is that, is that I grew up in a way that I'm blind to certain things in our society," Hamilton said during a sermon dubbed "Jesus, Protests and Repentance." "I just am. And I have certain benefits by virtue of being educated, White and male, right?" KANSAS DEMOCRAT BEGS KAMALA HARRIS NOT TO CAMPAIGN WITH HIM, ‘PLEASE DO NOT COME TO MY STATE’ "And we don't like to hear that, especially White folks don't like to hear that. But there are benefits that come along with that," he continued. Hamilton is running against Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in what has become one of the tightest races of this midterm cycle, despite Kansas' near-century-long history of not sending a Democratic candidate to the Senate. "Roger Marshall wants to talk about anything other than his history of suing and jailing mothers and protecting predators by voting against releasing the Epstein Files," Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton's campaign, told Fox News Digital. "Once again, he’s attacking Adam for something Roger said himself. Roger’s own pastor called Adam ‘middle of the road.’ Kansans are tired of high gas and grocery prices and ready for a senator who won’t divide us by race, religion, income, or ability to pay a medical bill at 18% interest." Republicans acknowledge that they are facing headwinds going into November’s election, but until recently, the contest between Marshall and Hamilton wasn’t of much concern for the GOP. SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL Now, the race has taken a turn and been rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report as voters fume over the cost of fuel, groceries and other economic pain. In response, national Republicans are beginning to dump more resources into the contest to ensure that they maintain the seat. Throughout the race, Marshall has largely aligned himself with President Donald Trump, only rarely breaking from the administration on certain decisions — last month he called for more advance notice and cooperation between the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Kansas government after federal immigration agents descended on the southern part of the state. Marshall has painted Hamilton as a "woke" megachurch pastor, delivering left-leaning ideals from the pulpit. 'JESUS WAS A RADICAL': PROGRESSIVES INVOKE CHRIST TO SELL LEFT-WING AGENDA ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL So has an outside group based in Massachusetts, the Main Street Fund, which ran an ad in Kansas that spliced portions of two different sermons and charged that Hamilton was "way too woke for Kansas," shortly after Hamilton won his primary, The Kansas City Star reported. During the sermon from June 2020 amid the Black Lives Matter (BLM) protests, Hamilton pushed back against rioting and looting, and argued that while the BLM movement was the focal point at the time, all lives matters. "Of course all lives matter," Hamilton said. "Everybody understands white lives matter, blue lives matter." Hamilton continued in his sermon posted on the church’s YouTube page in June 2020 amid the Black Lives Matter protests, "When I'm stopped by the police, I'm never afraid that they're gonna pull a gun on me." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But every African American man that I know is worried about what might happen when a police pull him over," Hamilton said at the time. "It's not that all the police are bad, they're gonna do something like that, but there's this fear underneath there. And so the hands go on the steering wheel at 10 and 2. They've been taught that from the time they were children. Right?" "I wasn't taught that, because I don't have to be afraid of that. Right? And there's a whole host of other things that are just a part of life. You know, I can ... well, you get the idea. There are benefits and privileges to my place in life. I have to recognize that," he continued. "To see that. And then I have to listen. I have to listen and understand, and finally be able to see the brokenness in myself, and my indifference. Before I can do anything to help anyone else, I have to have a conversion. I have to repent."And Marshall, who was running for his first term in the Senate at the time, struck a similar somber tone as Hamilton six years ago. In various posts to social media and interviews with local outlets, Marshall condemned Floyd's slaying and pushed for reforms that would ensure what happened in Minnesota and to federal Protective Services Officer Patrick Underwood, who was killed in a drive-by shooting just days after Floyd's death. "Additionally, Republicans called on Congressional Democrats to work across the aisle to make sure that what happened to George Floyd and Patrick Underwood never happens again, and significant bipartisan reform can be passed," Marshall said on Facebook following a House Judiciary hearing on police practices and law enforcement accountability.

news.title: MORNING GLORY: The polls got Michigan badly wrong. Now Democrats may face a bigger reckoning
news.text: The nationwide duel for the Senate is going on in the dark because polling this year has produced a series of spectacular busts, especially in Michigan, where polls on the primary battle between Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens posted double-digit lead after double-digit lead for El-Sayed. It is doubtful anyone following the news will stay home in Michigan in the general election. El-Sayed is — at best! — an Islamist apologist. He cannot own his past statements or campaign rhetoric. He refuses to discuss his most prominent supporter in the primary: far-left streamer and YouTube personality Hasan Piker, who is part crazy and part extremist. Piker carried El-Sayed over the finish line in the primary, but now voters are supposed to accept El-Sayed’s deflections when questioned about him. He’s done very little to hide his antipathy toward America’s ally Israel, going so far as to equate Israel with the Islamic Republic of Iran. Still, El-Sayed cannot simply declare that Israel is our ally and Iran is our enemy. That should tell everyone all they need to know about El-Sayed and cost him on November 3. EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER All across the country, Democrats have nominated candidates from the fringe, from El-Sayed in Michigan to James Talarico in Texas, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Troy Jackson in Maine. But El-Sayed is the worst of the lot…by a lot. And the stories keep coming as opposition research reveals facts about El-Sayed’s past that he has tried to hide, including his claim of dual citizenship, which he has subsequently repudiated. With nearly three weeks left before polls close, it’s fair to expect that more such old tape and tweets will surface. FETTERMAN 'DARES' EL-SAYED TO STICK WITH PIKER, CLAIMS MICHIGAN NOMINEE HAS 'LITTLE MAN SYNDROME ENERGY' El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, is, by contrast, a mainstream and moderate Michigander, a former FBI agent and lieutenant in the Army before he went on to serve in the Michigan legislature and then for more than a decade in the House of Representatives, finishing there as chairman of the House Intelligence Committee. news.title: Without social media I would not have this career: comedian Zarna Garg
news.text:
When your angelic goddaughter, who’s ever-so-slightly sceptical about your style of parenting, insists you watch every single clip of Zarna Garg, the Indian-American comedian “so much like you”, you can get a little prickly. What fresh meanness will this be? Garg is intense, real. Spills it all, relationships, kids. Makes you laugh through it all. Within two minutes of watching Garg’s skit as Nobel Peace Prize laureate Malala Yousafzai’s almost-therapist, you get the picture. 

Garg only began her career as a comedian at 43, after 16 years as a stay-at-home mother of three kids. Eight years later she’s had huge stand-up comedy success, opened for Tina Fey and Amy Poehler during their Restless Leg tour, created The Zarna Garg Family Podcast and written a New York Times bestseller (This American Woman); not to mention she has an enviable knack of getting us to laugh at ourselves. Angry about stereotypes? Garg embraces those stereotypes in the funniest way possible. If you ask me, inside every chill parent is an inner Garg wanting to get out.

Sure, there is a bit of bothsidesism: she praised both Kamala Harris and Usha Vance before 2024’s US presidential election, and last year she took part in Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh Comedy Festival, an event we hardly needed Human Rights Watch to tell us: “This whitewashing comes amid significant increase in repression, including a crackdown on free speech, which many of these comedians defend but people in Saudi Arabia are completely denied.” Garg stood by her decision.

Now, she is coming to Australia with her Million Dollar Excuses tour in November and December. By early September she’d already sold out four Sydney shows without a whisper of publicity. Then the Opera House added a Studio date, and Melbourne went bonkers for her, adding a show at the Palais to the two at the National.
news.summary: The Indian-American comedian is bringing her ferocious domestic wit to Australia.
news.author: Jenna Price
