news.title: Donald Trump Voter Who Trusted Him ‘1,000%’ Changes His Tune In Revealing Radio Call
news.text:
SiriusXM’s “The Megyn Kelly Wrap-Up Show” on Wednesday invited yet another disillusioned Donald Trump voter on air to vent about the president ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

This time, it was John from Pennsylvania’s turn to explain to host Emily Jashinsky exactly why he is “angry” with the man he helped back into office and admitted he still calls “Big Daddy Trump.”

“I’m self-employed. My insurance, my health insurance has turned into, now, like a huge mortgage payment with a huge deductible. I have two 16-year-old boys that just started driving on my insurance as well. That’s insane. Gas prices are insane,” he said in audio shared online by the nonprofit research center Media Matters for America.

John voted for Trump, who is currently enduring some of the worst polling numbers of his presidency, in the 2024 election and said he was “horrified at the thought” of Trump’s rival, former Vice President Kamala Harris, winning the White House, he told Jashinsky.

“But I got to tell you, I’m angry,” he continued, adding that he “trusted Trump” and “it’s so weird because I supported him completely, I trusted him 1,000%.”

John said his “one fear, was my insurance and stuff like that, and I’m getting clobbered now, and it’s hard to make ends meet.”

“My wife also, she’s self-employed. We’re struggling,” he added. “And they talk about, like, kitchen table issues. This is a huge one for me.”

John revealed that politically he’s “up in the air right now.”

“I grew up as, my household, my dad was an old-school Democrat union guy. I believe that barely even, it doesn’t exist anymore,” he said. “And I don’t mean to sound mean, but I’m not a, you know, the blue-haired liberals and this weird nonsense. I’m not down with that. But I feel, I don’t want to say lied to, but I’m upset.”

Listen here via Media Matters for America

news.title: Donald Trump cancels trip to Bucs-Steelers NFL game this weekend hours after CNN revealed his plans
news.text:
Donald Trump has canceled plans to attend a second football game in as many weeks, according to a report. 

One week after being forced to back out of attending the SEC showdown between Georgia and Alabama, the President has reportedly canceled a trip to an NFL game. 

CNN reported on Tuesday afternoon that Trump was expected to attend the Week 6 clash between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium in Florida on Sunday. 

However, the President seemingly pulled a quick U-turn, with the outlet reporting a matter of hours later that he would no longer attend the game. 

The matchup would have marked the second Steelers game that Trump has been in the stands for in two years. 

He also attended the Steelers’ matchup against the New York Jets at Acrisure Stadium in 2024 during his Presidential campaign against Kamala Harris. Pittsburgh proved to be a crucial swing state for the Republican party in the election. 

The U-turn comes less than a week after Trump was also forced to scrap his visit to the college football game between Georgia and Alabama. 

The trip was cancelled due to the arrival of Hurricane Isaias, a Category 3 storm, which made landfall on the Alabama coast on Friday evening.

'Based on the fact that a huge Hurricane/Storm is coming, it is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!' Trump posted to his Truth Social account on October 9.

'Therefore, I will miss that potentially unbelievable Game, Alabama vs. Georgia but, hopefully, the Game will go on despite the weather! I will be visiting both of those Teams at a later date.'

The southeast of the US has been ravaged by Hurricane Isaias after it hit last Friday night, leaving four people dead and others injured.

The monster storm hit the Florida Panhandle near Destin at around 8.30pm as a Category 2 hurricane, packing maximum sustained winds of 105mph. 

Just 30 minutes later, its winds had fallen to 85mph, but the storm continued to wreak havoc along the Gulf Coast.

The rivalry clash between the Bulldogs and the Crimson Tide still went ahead in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, with the President missing out on a thrilling game. 

Georgia emerged as 20-17 winners at Bryant-Denny Stadium after a controversial finish that saw fans furious at the SEC officials.

With 3:28 left in the game and down by three, Alabama quarterback Keelon Russell fired a second-down pass towards Rico Scott in the end zone.

But Georgia defensive back KJ Bolden didn't play the ball and made contact with Scott without turning his head to the backfield.

Those watching all waited for a flag to be thrown but officials determined it was not pass interference. The next play, Russell was sacked to move them out of field goal range, then Alabama punted and never got the ball back.

Head coach Kaleb DeBoer raged on the sidelines as officials decided not to throw a flag, while ESPN/ABC rules analyst Matt Austin saw a new angle as the Bulldogs kneeled out the clock to end the game.
news.summary: One week after being forced to back out of attending the SEC showdown between Georgia and Alabama, the President has reportedly canceled a trip to an NFL game this weekend.

news.title: Tension erupts during House midterm debate as Lawler fact-checks NY Democrat opponent on immigration
news.text:
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., faced off against Democrat opponent Cait Conley Wednesday night in a one-hour debate filled with interruptions and fiery accusations less than three weeks before Election Day.

Lawler is vying for a third term representing New York’s 17th Congressional District, a politically moderate area in the New York City suburbs that could decide the fate of who controls the House of Representatives for the final years of President Donald Trump’s term.

Lawler called out Conley for misrepresenting his voting record, Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and her own stance on immigration enforcement. Conley, meanwhile, tried to paint Lawler as a Trump acolyte who put the needs of Washington Republicans ahead of the people of his district.

Their most heated clashes came on the immigration front, when the moderator referenced the recent shooting of an illegal immigrant by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents last week in New York City while the man’s 5-year-old child was in the car.

DEM CANDIDATE CLEARS CROWDED FIELD TO FACE TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT IN NY

The race between GOP Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat veteran Cait Conley could decide the fate of the House of Representatives for the next two years. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

“I believe that border security is national security and that we do need immigration enforcement to ensure that violent criminals and drug cartels and human traffickers and terrorist organizations aren’t in our communities and that they are deported,” Conley said. 

“But what we are seeing right now with the conduct of ICE is posing a public safety hazard. To your point, last week, they shot into a car where there was a 5-year-old child. I’ll tell you, as a law enforcement officer, you’re not permitted to do that kind of stuff.”

NEW YORK GOVERNOR DEBATE HEATS UP AS BLAKEMAN, HOCHUL SPAR OVER TRUMP, SANCTUARY STATUS, ICE SHOOTING

Lawler, however, pointed out the man has a lengthy criminal rap sheet and was seen by some as a danger to his community. He also argued the shooting would never have happened had local law enforcement not been barred from handing him over to ICE by New York’s sanctuary laws.

He said Conley “supports making New York a sanctuary state, prohibits cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration officials.”

WATCH: LAWLER UNLOADS ON RASKIN AFTER FIERY IMMIGRATION HEARING: ‘GROW THE F— UP’

Lawler later pivoted the discussion to Sheridan Gorman, the college student from his district who was killed while out with her friends near her campus in Chicago earlier this year. The illegal immigrant accused of killing her was previously charged with shoplifting, but Chicago sanctuary laws prevent local law enforcement from handing him over to ICE.

Police tape cordons off a street in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx after a shooting involving federal law enforcement agents last week. (WCBS)

Conley called Gorman’s death “an atrocious crime” while repeatedly pointing out it took place in Chicago.

Lawler attempted to intervene multiple times to call it “preventable,” to which an irate Conley responded, “Can I finish?”

“And I do support federal agents and federal law enforcement, federal immigration enforcement, making sure that we deport violent citizens,” she said.

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO ‘WITHHOLD FUNDING’ FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Lawler then argued, however, that Conley’s support of sanctuary policies runs counter to that.

“If you think he should have been deported when he was arrested for shoplifting, he should have been turned over to ICE. Under the new law that you support, he will not be turned over to ICE, and he will be released under cashless bail,” Lawler said.

It prompted the moderator to step in, telling Lawler there was no “cross-examination round.”

Elsewhere in the debate, Lawler accused Conley of having “literally just lied” that Lawler voted with Trump “100% of the time.”

10 DEMOCRAT-HELD HOUSE SEATS REPUBLICANS COULD FLIP TO SAVE THEIR MAJORITY

“I’ve been rated the third most independent member of my conference. And I have taken on the president on numerous issues, including lifting the cap on SALT, including extending Haitian TPS, including passing an extension for the ACA enhanced premium tax credit despite his objections,” Lawler said.

Earlier in the debate, Conley tried to accuse Lawler of supporting tax breaks for companies that build data centers as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill.

Sheridan Gorman and her father, Tom Gorman, in a family photo. (Gorman Family/Fox News)

Lawler shot back, “I know you just moved here from Virginia, so it’s hard for you to understand the local communities, but the fact is … the provision you referenced in the Working Families Tax Cut Act is $80 billion for 100% expensing for every business in America to expense plant, property and equipment. 

“Are you against our small businesses in the Hudson Valley being able to expense their plant, property and equipment and hire more people? Your attack on that rings hollow. You clearly don’t understand what’s actually in the tax bill. And part of the problem is you don’t pay property taxes.”

Both candidates shook hands after their spirited debate and thanked each other for appearing. Lawler also thanked Conley for her military service.

The district is a pivotal one for control of the House next year. Lawler is one of three House Republicans who won a district that former Vice President Kamala Harris also won in 2024. 

And in an election that’s expected to be brutal for the GOP, both sides are pouring millions of dollars into the fight.

news.text:
The Democratic Party is sending a veteran to the front lines.

Former President Bill Clinton, 80, will join Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly at an evening interfaith event in Hollywood, Florida, next week, according to MS NOW.

Jolly, a former Republican congressman, easily won the Democratic nomination in April and is facing a heated matchup against Republican Rep. Byron Donalds to succeed Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Clinton is making his first public campaign appearance only two weeks before the midterm elections, similar to how he campaigned in 2022. In the days leading up to the 2022 midterms, Clinton rallied Democrats in New York, New Jersey, and South Texas.

However, the 42nd POTUS was much busier in 2024, making dozens of appearances to support then-Vice President Kamala Harris and campaigning for multiple down-ballot Democrats.

Earlier this week, he appeared alongside Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries at a fundraiser in New York to support Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz. The Florida congressman is running in a newly remapped district after DeSantis signed a new congressional map into law in May.

Similar to President Donald Trump, Clinton has faced scrutiny over his relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

In February, he was brought in for a closed-door deposition by the House Oversight Committee as part of a probe into the Epstein files, which included photos of the former president alongside Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and numerous unidentified women.

Clinton insisted he did nothing wrong and had “no idea” about any of the crimes Epstein committed. He added that he saw nothing that “ever gave me pause.”

“As someone who grew up in a home with domestic abuse, not only would I not have flown on his plane if I had any inkling of what he was doing—I would have turned him in myself and led the call for justice for his crimes, not sweetheart deals,” he said in a statement shared on X at the time.

Government-released documents revealed Clinton traveled on Epstein’s private jet, nicknamed the Lolita Express, 16 times.

However, even Trump, 80, felt sympathy for his Democratic adversary.

“I don’t like seeing him deposed,” Trump said of Clinton at the time. “But they certainly went after me a lot more than that.”

Trump did not extend the same sympathy to Clinton’s wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who was also deposed the day before her husband.

news.title: El-Sayed’s ‘Medicare for All’ Plays Well With Voters. It Won’t If It Ever Becomes Law.
news.text:
In 2013, Abdul El-Sayed was a young man with a fiery pen and a conviction that the recently reelected President Barack Obama was “not the right choice” for the country. “He just wasn’t the wrong one.” 

The problem? Young El-Sayed didn’t think Obama was progressive enough. “Take healthcare, his prized accomplishment, for example: it’s a watered-down reform that kowtows to the interests of healthcare lobbies before it provides meaningful, secure access to healthcare for our society’s most desperate,” he wrote at the Huffington Post. 

To his credit, Obama, apparently, didn’t hold a 13-year grudge. Although he didn’t endorse El-Sayed in the primary, he has deigned to appear on the campaign trail next week to try to convince Michiganders to vote for his former detractor. Judging by Obama’s comments thus far, his pitch will be that El-Sayed is a true-blue Democrat cut from the old cloth rather than a champion of Woke 2.0.

In fact, when Politico asked Obama about his decision to endorse El-Sayed in the general Michigan Senate race, the former president pushed back on the claim that the Muslim doctor is radical at all: “I don’t know, he’s for a higher minimum wage and health care for all, and it doesn’t seem crazy to me. You know, FDR was for that too.” 

There’s a lot of political craftiness in that sentence. Obviously, Obama is comparing El-Sayed to a generally well-regarded Democratic president and conveniently ignoring El-Sayed’s support for such policies as putting boys in girls’ locker rooms, defunding the police, and freeing Palestine. Simultaneously, he’s also harping on issues voters care about a great deal. Health care, especially, is a big issue — bigger, perhaps, than we’d like to admit. 

According to recent numbers from KFF Polling, more than half the country says it is “very concerned” or “somewhat concerned” about its health care costs (insurance, prescription drugs, out-of-pocket costs, etc). Meanwhile, just under half of Republicans, Democrats, and Independents told the Commonwealth Fund that premiums were their top concern when it came to health care. 

Unfortunately, those premiums are top of mind for most people right now. In just the past year, 59 percent of Americans saw premium costs rise, and 41 percent of Americans saw them rise by more than 10 percent.

So when El-Sayed and his strategists started looking around for a central plank for his senatorial campaign, Medicare for All (a plan Bernie Sanders hatched a long time ago and that currently has the support of 14 sitting senators) seemed like a good thing to focus on. 

The problem is that Medicare for All is not universally popular. And El-Sayed knows it. 

The Commonwealth Fund found that just a bare majority of Americans think the federal government should step in and fix the health care system. That’s a majority, yes, but a politician also has to contend with everyone else.

Perhaps those statistics (or statistics like them) were going through El-Sayed’s brain when he stood up on the NBC debate stage a few days ago and told voters that they could keep their private insurance under Medicare for All if they so desired. The trouble is, the actual bill itself doesn’t allow for that, and as Deroy Murdock pointed out at this outlet just a few days ago, his assurances to the contrary directly contradict earlier statements he’s made. 

In fact, those 49 percent of Americans who are skeptical of the federal government’s ability to fix the health care problem are right to be so wary. The plan is prohibitively expensive. Because Sanders has been on the warpath for universal health care for quite a long time, plenty of experts have already crunched the numbers. 

Back in 2019, the Heritage Foundation concluded that the government would have to impose serious tax hikes on the average American to fund Medicare for All. So much so that households that currently rely on employer-sponsored health insurance (most of them) would see a net $13,909 less in disposable income adjusted to reflect current dollar valuations (or $10,554 in 2019’s figures). That means less money for things like dinners out, concert tickets, or Christmas gifts — all the stuff that keeps the economy doing its thing. 

More recently, the American Action Forum calculated the cost of a similar Medicare for All program proposed by Kamala Harris and found that it will cost the U.S. taxpayer $2.5 trillion in 2027 and up to $5.9 trillion in 2036. The two plans function on much the same premise: namely, that the government should offer health insurance to anyone who wants it. 

To be fair to El-Sayed, he does sort of have a plan to make the whole thing less onerous for most of us: “Tax. Billionaire. Wealth.” But, as Byron York recently wrote at the Washington Examiner, you simply couldn’t tax the billionaires enough to pay for the system, so that solution is hardly feasible.

A KFF poll released earlier this month found that voters generally favor universal healthcare promises — until they hear about its downsides. They’d oppose it even more if they had to live those downsides. 

H. L. Mencken once observed, “Democracy is the theory that the common people know what they want, and deserve to get it good and hard.” At this point, all we can do is hope that the allure of “free” health care doesn’t blind Michiganders to reality as they head to the ballot box.

news.title: The Democrat Campaign to Destroy Kamala Harris
news.text:
Democrats simply do not want Kamala Harris to run for president. After seeing her flub her 2020 presidential campaign, flounder in embarrassing stories as vice president, and — most critically — lose in 2024 to Donald Trump, they’re sick of her. They have adopted in full force the Republican talking point that Kamala Harris is an awful politician.

A Politico article published yesterday reveals that a full 20 Democratic politicians and strategists have told them that Kamala Harris failed epically at defining herself in 2026. It was, the publication concluded, a “wasted year” for her in which she did nothing to stake out a position in the intra-Democratic Party debates.

Among these 20 is former South Carolina Gov. Jim Hodges. He said that Harris’ politicking these days “seems like more of the same to me.” That’s a problem, he said, because Democrats want someone who is “fresh, new.” He said, “I hear a lot of talk about that — ‘we don’t need recycled candidates.’”

Even more brutal was Doug Herman, a former political strategist for Barack Obama.

“She totally blew it,” he said of Kamala’s year. “She hasn’t gotten into the mix.”

Kamala Harris has never been a particularly talented politician, especially when it comes to having a coherent vision, giving people a cause to believe in, or associating herself with memorable policy goals.

Look at how many unpopular policy positions she has taken and then awkwardly backed away from. In the 2019 Democratic primary campaign, Harris raised her hand to say she wanted to outlaw private health insurance before walking it back the next morning and claiming she hadn’t understood the question. Also in 2019, she told MSNBC that she thought the U.S. should “probably think about starting from scratch” on immigration laws. Her campaign website, meanwhile, stated, “[W]e must fundamentally overhaul our immigration enforcement policies and practices — they are cruel and out of control.” And yet as vice president and border czar, she made vague statements that immigration was due to “root causes” while allowing it to run uncontrolled, before claiming that she was doing everything she could to stop illegal immigration.

Those aren’t the only policy areas where Kamala Harris has looked hapless. During her 2024 presidential election, Harris decided to make her support for the mass murder of unborn children the primary focus of her campaign. “[M]y first priority is to put back in place those protections and to stop this pain,” she said at one campaign rally. (Apparently the pain children feel in the womb doesn’t count.) This ended up being less than appealing to the majority of Americans; only 14 percent said abortion was their top issue.

When voters look at Kamala Harris’ time as vice president, not much comes to mind when the question of her accomplishments is raised. When Harris was running for president, this was a perennial concern for party officials. Donna Brazil, the former chair of the Democratic National Committee, even penned a piece in the New York Times answering to this concern with a bevy of excuses. “A vice president is expected to never disagree with the president in public and must make the president look good without claiming personal credit for accomplishments,” she said. “Yet when running for president, a vice president gets no credit from opponents for administration successes, but instead is blamed for supposed administration failures.”

Worse for Harris, it sounds like the donors are not on her side. They don’t want to put their money behind the woman who lost to Donald Trump.

A “California-based fundraiser” told Politico that there is no one among their circle of donors who wants to support Kamala Harris.

“She probably could raise grassroots money because she has fabulous lists,” the person said. “But there are no obvious big donors that have indicated they want to go down that route.”

Laurie Black, a former Harris donor, publicly told Politico that she’s done with Harris. “I want to support a winner in 2028,” she said, “and I just don’t know if the vice president has the juice this time.”

The Wall Street Journal likewise reported last week that donors have told Harris in no uncertain terms that her campaign would have a hard time winning. They, the Journal reported, “have told her directly that a bid would be a long shot.”

There is reason to believe that Harris will listen to what the donors are telling her and decide to not run for president. “Some people who have known and worked with Harris are skeptical she will ultimately mount another run,” the Wall Street Journal reported.

Perhaps Gavin Newsom has insider knowledge that Kamala Harris will indeed not run for president. In a recent interview with Jake Tapper, he said that he won’t run for president if Kamala Harris runs for president — and Gavin Newsom is most decidedly running for president. He himself openly speculated that he could announce his presidential bid before the end of 2026. In an interview with the Associated Press, he said in response to the question of whether he would announce his campaign before the end of the year: “It’s the right question. Honestly, I don’t know. I think this thing’s happening. I mean, you already feel it, right?” (READ MORE: Newsom Performs Another Political Stunt)

There is also what Harris’ husband said about her. Last week, the Wall Street Journal reported that Doug Emhoff “shared concerns with others about another run.” According to Harris’ book, her presidential campaign was a strain on their marriage. It is likely that Democrats who heard this from Emhoff ratted him out to the Wall Street Journal to make Kamala look bad.

Still, even if Democratic party officials want nothing to do with her anymore, Harris does lead early polls of Democratic primary candidates.

news.title: Canadian singer Joni Mitchell officially becomes American citizen after 62-year journey
news.text: Joni Mitchell has officially become an American citizen at age 82, more than six decades after she first moved to the United States. The music icon, who hails from Canada, announced the news on Instagram, sharing a photo of herself beaming while holding an American flag along with a video from her naturalization ceremony. "A journey that began 62 years ago," Mitchell wrote in the caption of her post. ART GARFUNKEL JOINS GROWING LIST OF CELEBRITIES CONSIDERING A MOVE ABROAD OVER TRUMP PRESIDENCY Mitchell wore a red and navy blue floral cardigan that had an American flag pin along with a red beaded necklace, a red beret and black pants with black boots while posing in between an American flag and a Department of Homeland Security flag. In the video Mitchell uploaded, she was seated in the front row at the ceremony as the speaker announced, "And Joni Mitchell, Canada" to cheers and applause from the audience. According to KSL, Mitchell will also retain her Canadian citizenship because the U.S. and Canada legally permit dual citizenship. The legendary singer-songwriter was born Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, Alberta, to Royal Canadian Air Force flight Lt. William Andrew Anderson and teacher Myrtle Marguerite. Mitchell's family lived on several bases during World War II before eventually settling in Saskatoon, which the singer has often referred to as her hometown. She went on to attend the Alberta College of Art in Calgary before dropping out and relocating to Toronto, where she played gigs at coffee houses and folk clubs. The "Both Sides Now" songstress moved to the United States in 1965 at age 21 after marrying American folk singer Chuck Mitchell. The former couple, who lived in Detroit, Michigan, performed together as a folk duo before divorcing in 1967. After their divorce, Mitchell left Detroit and moved to New York City, where she became part of the Greenwich Village folk scene and performed along the East Coast. By 1968, Mitchell moved to Los Angeles, settling in Laurel Canyon, which was becoming a hub for singer-songwriters including David Crosby, Graham Nash and others. In the mid-1970s, Mitchell moved to LA's Bel Air neighborhood, where she lived in a historic 1920s home for decades. Mitchell built her legendary music career while living in California, where she recorded many of her most acclaimed albums, including "Blue," "Court and Spark" and "Ladies of the Canyon." Mitchell has won 11 Grammy Awards and was inducted into both the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1997. She was also recognized with the Kennedy Center Honors in 2021 and received the prestigious Library of Congress Gershwin Prize for Popular Song in 2023. The musician lives in Santa Barbara, California. Mitchell is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and expressed frustration that she couldn't vote in U.S. elections because she was Canadian. After singing a lyric about wealthy financiers, she added, "Like Donald Trump!" Following her performance of the song, Mitchell responded to an audience member who shouted an anti-Trump remark. "'F--- Donald Trump.' I love that song," she said, apparently referencing rapper YG's 2016 protest song "FDT (F--- Donald Trump)" featuring the late rapper and activist Nipsey Hussle. She then encouraged Americans to participate in the 2024 U.S. presidential election, in which Trump ran against Democratic nominee former Vice President Kamala Harris. "Everybody get out and vote. This is an important one. I wish I could vote . I'm Canadian. I'm one of those lousy immigrants," Mitchell said. Months before becoming an American citizen, Mitchell criticized the political climate in the U.S. while accepting a lifetime achievement award at Canada's Juno Awards in March. At the ceremony, Mitchell praised Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, saying, "I'm so glad to be back in Canada. This man is a blessing. You guys are so fortunate." After Mitchell's comments at the Juno Awards, the White House issued a dismissive response. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? news.title: Democrats Turn to Bill Clinton for Late Campaign Push in Florida
news.text:
Former President Bill Clinton is joining Florida Democrats’ late push for votes, with a campaign appearance for gubernatorial nominee David Jolly scheduled two weeks before Election Day.

Clinton will appear alongside Jolly at an evening interfaith event in Hollywood on Tuesday, October 20. The visit will mark his first public campaign stop of the 2026 midterms, according to Jolly’s campaign.

The former president’s appearance comes as Jolly, a former Republican congressman who won the Democrat nomination in August, faces Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in the race to replace outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Democrats are bringing Clinton into a state where they have struggled for decades to win the governor’s office. Lawton Chiles was the last Democrat elected governor of Florida, winning reelection in 1994. Jolly is seeking to break that streak on November 3, but recent surveys offer different pictures of his chances against Donalds.

Clinton’s visit comes after a Stetson University poll released Tuesday showed Donalds ahead of Jolly by 11 points, 52% to 41%, among modeled likely voters. Other polling has shown a narrower contest. A St. Pete Polls survey conducted October 5–7 put the candidates at 45% each, while a YouGov survey released last week showed Donalds ahead 47% to 45%.

Clinton’s visit will take place as early voting begins in parts of Florida, giving Jolly a prominent Democrat surrogate during the final stretch of the campaign. The governor’s race is also drawing attention beyond the state.

The Cook Political Report moved the contest from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican” earlier this month, keeping Republicans favored while acknowledging a more competitive race. The change came despite Donalds’ substantial financial advantage over Jolly. Clinton’s help for Florida Democrats extends beyond the governor’s contest.

Clinton and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries headlined a New York fundraiser earlier this week for Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-FL), MS NOW reported. Moskowitz is seeking reelection in a newly drawn district described by the outlet as a toss-up after a DeSantis-backed congressional remapping altered his previous seat.

The former president has made similar late appearances in previous elections. During the 2022 midterms, he campaigned in New York, New Jersey, and South Texas in the closing days before voters went to the polls.

He took on a larger role in 2024, making dozens of campaign stops across battleground states for then-Vice President Kamala Harris while also supporting candidates further down the ballot.

news.title: Trump's sham 'peace plan' for Palestine is a year old, more than 1,500 have been killed in Gaza since
news.text:
There have been many shameful days in the history of American foreign policy, but one was this time last year when President Donald Trump visited Israel and Egypt to promote his ‘comprehensive’ peace plan. Many thought it a sham; the last year has proven it so.

At least 1,480 civilians have been killed in Gaza since then, 320 of them children. More than 5,000 have been seriously injured. Four Israeli soldiers were killed; independent sources say the IDF mounted 4,000 attacks on Gaza over that time. Numerous sources have verified that Israel targeted aid convoys and humanitarian buffer zones, significantly increasing the number of fatalities.

The 1,480 killed may appear unremarkable against the c.80,000 (with thousands more under the 60 million tonnes of rubble) slaughtered over the first two years of the genocide. Official data suggests otherwise.

In the eight years before 2023, the number of Palestinians killed each year in Gaza was a fraction of the total killed in the 12 months since Trump announced his ‘comprehensive’ peace. In fact, the number killed in the last year is twice the total number of Palestinians that Israel killed between 2015 and 2022. 

Israel is actively degrading life for the 2.1 million Palestinians who survive. It has tightened its control over 65% of Gaza, herding the indigenous people into the remaining 35%. 80% of Gaza’s buildings have been destroyed: most of its schools and its hospitals cannot function. 

 There is no peace, never mind a comprehensive one.

Most of the institutional West latched onto Trump’s plan; even Palestine’s greatest European ally, Spanish PM Pedro Sanchez, chose to be in Sharm el-Sheikh for its official unveiling. That was the second element of the day’s pageantry; one that Trump’s earlier address to Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, rendered meaningless. 

The eulogistic tone of all those who spoke would have embarrassed many, but not Trump. Knesset speaker Amir Ohana went back two-and-a-half millennia to compare him to Cyrus the Great. 

Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Yair Lapid were no less fulsome; Lapid reminded the world why Israel’s rights, found in the Book of Genesis, are non-negotiable: "And I will give you, and your descendants after you, the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession”. 

Israel, expecting a peace plan centred on its interests, was not to be disappointed! Trump’s own speech took over an hour to deliver. Palestine and its people were mentioned only once, when, without a hint of irony, he said that provided they committed to peace, Palestinians might expect "a return to the basics of life". 

Their cause is hopeless as long as America is in control.

Trump and his team of advisers' real ambition was clear; his cabal of son-in-law Jared Kushner, acolyte Steve Witkoff, and global diplomatic wizard Tony Blair made little effort to camouflage it. Team Trump wants to transform Gaza’s rubble into an economic boom for the US, its western and Arab allies and the Trump family. 

There was one truth in Trump’s remarks: that since Israel’s foundation, the US had partnered with it "through thick and thin…through glory and heartache". This has been different, though. Never before has that support directly facilitated the slaughter of tens of thousands of civilians. 

Since its foundation in 1948, Israel has received more than $300 billion in military and financial aid from the US, averaging about $3.2bn a year; over the last three years, it has received $32bn, or about $10.6bn annually. 

When Joe Biden, in October 2023, promised "unprecedented" levels of support, he sparked a genocide that is as much America’s as it is Israel’s. We shouldn’t forget that Joe Biden, a self-declared zionist, his vice president Kamala Harris and secretary of state Anthony Blinken formed an unprecedented phalanx of support for Israel. 

Trump’s strongly pro-Israel first term suggested no change when he regained office in 2024; in truth, the only difference between him and Biden has been style. Trump’s Knesset address a year ago endorsed Netanyahu’s claim that he had "won" and committed to working with him to make Israel "stronger, and bigger and better than it’s ever been before". 

Proceedings in Israel’s parliament on October 13, 2025, showed the West was prepared to praise and reward settler-colonial Israel for its brutal subjugation of the Palestinians. Only Trump could have described the genocide as a "victory" for Israel. 

Only Trump could have touted a peace plan that was so obviously centred on wealth-creation for Israel, its allies and his own family. Only Trump could have declared the rebuilding of Gaza for the benefit of monied Western and Arab nations and private interests a "comprehensive peace".

Some nations refused to join his peace board, but few analysed the plan or highlighted its malign intent. America’s president made no effort to hide its ambition. 

It would breathe life into the zionist idyll of greater Israel, but the transformation would do more than deliver that political outcome; it would create a regional economic powerhouse that would enrich his Arab allies and, of course, his own family. Trump and those backing him see no irony in backing the zionist determination to build greater Israel from the Nile to the Euphrates while criminalising those who support Palestine by chanting "from the river to the sea".

Israel is inherently expansionist; without that fundamental being challenged, nothing will change. Trump’s address to the Knesset and his faux peace plan, formalised a year ago, represent a chilling exposition of contemporary Western colonialism. 

In the Knesset, a US president greenlit the ultimate zionist ambition. Largely courtesy of the United States, the institutional West’s disinterest in the truth remains intact as the genocide continues.

news.text:
Four years later, Guilfoyle had become less helper than headache. Trump, Jr., had been seen with another woman, a Palm Beach socialite to whom he is now married, and the couple’s engagement was called off. “I had to get her out of here,” Trump reportedly told people. (The White House has denied that Trump made this statement.) The solution: naming Guilfoyle Ambassador to Greece, a country with which she had no clear ties—her mother is from Puerto Rico, her father from Ireland—but that became, or so it appeared, a convenient place to stash the inconvenient ex.
Those who had paid attention to Guilfoyle’s past might have questioned her diplomatic skills. She was forced to leave Fox in 2018 over allegations of questionable workplace behavior. Two years later, my colleague Jane Mayer reported on the details: one of Guilfoyle’s assistants had accused her of repeated sexual harassment. The assistant, Mayer wrote, claimed to have been subject to “degrading, abusive, and sexually inappropriate behavior; among other things, she said that she was frequently required to work at Guilfoyle’s New York apartment while the Fox host displayed herself naked, and was shown photographs of the genitalia of men with whom Guilfoyle had had sexual relations.” (Guilfoyle denied wrongdoing.) Fox paid “upward of four million dollars” to settle the complaint.
On Tuesday, Guilfoyle was forced to resign from the ambassadorship a year into the post, for problems of a different nature: financial, not sexual, although her provocative attire as Ambassador also drew attention. (Among other fashion choices, Guilfoyle, who travels with a stylist, wore a see-through black lace dress to a Thanksgiving dinner hosted by the American-Hellenic Chamber of Commerce.) The Wall Street Journal had published a devastating trio of stories about Guilfoyle’s behavior on the job. First came a piece in late September about Guilfoyle’s unusually dogged advocacy on behalf of a Greek construction firm, the Aktor Group, which was seeking to break into the energy business; Christos Marafatsos, a top lobbyist for the company, “has attended so many of her meetings that some foreign officials mistook him for her chief of staff,” the Journal wrote. (Aktor and attorneys for Guilfoyle have denied any improprieties.) Then, last week, the Journal reported on Guilfoyle’s beseeching a Trump donor to wire her a hundred thousand dollars to pay her American Express bill in advance of her confirmation hearing. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” Guilfoyle texted the donor, Eric Deters, adding a prayer-hands emoji. Deters, a Kentucky lawyer and former congressional candidate, had already paid Guilfoyle three hundred thousand dollars; among other things he sought a meeting with the commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service to discuss his tax problems. “As of this memo, I have not received one favor,” Deters wrote. “I am not naive or a sucker. I need results.”
Guilfoyle, a lawyer and former prosecutor—she overlapped with Kamala Harris in the San Francisco district attorney’s office—understood the risk posed by Deters’s digital trail. “Stop papering all these things,” she warned, advising Deters to call her on Signal instead. “It’s really dangerous.” Deters ultimately balked at the AmEx payment. “I can’t do this without getting a divorce,” he told Guilfoyle. (Guilfoyle has suggested the texts were generated by A.I. and said, “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”)
The Journal’s final blow, on Saturday, described how Guilfoyle accepted luxury travel, including from a Greek shipping magnate who hosted Guilfoyle on his private jet and paid her bill at the Four Seasons Hotel George V, in Paris, while she was in town to attend his wife’s fashion show. Lobbying an unnamed U.S. businessman to secure an invitation to a dinner at the World Economic Forum in Davos in honor of Eric Trump, Guilfoyle promised, “I’m going to make you a lot of fucking money,” according to a recording reviewed by the Journal.
The paradox of Trump Administration corruption is that the most egregious offenders—the President chief among them—operate in plain sight and on a grand scale. They don’t fret, to borrow Guilfoyle’s verb, about “papering” the evidence; they consider themselves, perhaps with good reason, immune from consequences. To borrow from Nixon’s answer to David Frost, when the President does it, that means it is not grifting. Trump imposed some constraints on his own and his immediate family’s dealings during his first term—he promised, for example, that the Trump Organization would not conduct business abroad—but these limits, such as they were, have been shrugged off in the second. As Trump explained to the Times in January, “I found out that nobody cared. . . . I got absolutely no credit for it.”
My colleague David Kirkpatrick calculated that during the first year of his second term, Trump and his family leveraged the Presidency to make more than four billion dollars, dealing in cryptocurrency, foreign real-estate investments, and prediction markets. That total does not include the potential value of Trump’s collusive “settlement” of a private lawsuit against the I.R.S. for the leak of his tax information; as part of the arrangement, the government agreed that Trump, his family, and his companies would be immune from back taxes and penalties. Meanwhile, the President’s son-in-law Jared Kushner is both an unpaid negotiator for the Trump Administration and the owner of an investment firm, Affinity Partners, that is almost entirely financed by Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries.
When there are consequences for Trump family members’ overreach, they tend toward the minimum. Last month, ProPublica reported that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin had paid hundreds of thousands in expenses for Donald Trump, Jr., and his new wife, Bettina Anderson Trump’s May wedding celebration, including renting out a private island and putting on a fireworks display. The President described this arrangement as “very common” and “totally allowed,” but said his son was repaying the oligarch. Contrast that seeming nonchalance with Trump’s response to reports of profiteering by James Blair and Chris LaCivita, two of his senior political advisers. On October 6th, the Times reported that, in the heat of the U.S. midterm campaign, the pair had travelled to Republika Srpska, a self-governing territory in the Balkans, to help the pro-Russia government in advance of its own elections. Blair, the former deputy White House chief of staff, and LaCivita, a co-manager of Trump’s 2024 campaign, were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars through a Washington law firm, the Times said. Trump, typically, diminished his relationship with the two men, calling them “outside consultants” who “do not work for me.” He added, “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”
Guilfoyle would seem to require particularly careful handling. Having dated Don, Jr., for years, she presumably knows a lot of Trump family and Trump business secrets. So it was something of a surprise that the White House opted not to accord her the ordinary face-saving courtesy of announcing her own departure. Instead, the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, said Guilfoyle had been asked to resign. Zacharia added, incongruously, “She has been a wonderful asset to the team.” What, one wonders, would count as a liability? ♦
news.summary: In this Administration, former Ambassador Guilfoyle is the rare Trump associate to face consequences for misdeeds.

news.title: Republicans Get New Midterm Warning Sign as Kansas Senate Race Shifts
news.text: Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball has shifted numerous U.S. Senate races in favor of Democrats on Wednesday, including Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall's seat in Kansas versus Democrat Adam Hamilton. The forecaster has moved the race from Leans Republican to a Toss-Up. Marshall, a doctor, is currently in the seat that has been held by the GOP since 1919, the longest ever for any party. In a post on Truth Social discussing a potential rally for Marshall in the near future, President Donald Trump called him one of his "favorite Senators." Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. Trump carried Kansas by double digits over then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, underscoring the state’s Republican tilt. But Democrats have maintained a foothold in the state, with Laura Kelly in the governor’s mansion even as Republicans hold both U.S. Senate seats. Hamilton campaign spokesperson Glynnis Harvey told Newsweek when asked about the new shift from Sabato’s Crystal Ball, "Roger Marshall abandoned Kansas. Instead of fighting for Kansas farmers, aviation workers, and families, he’s been a yes-man to corruption in Washington, supporting policies that are driving up costs and cutting healthcare. Republicans, Democrats, and Independents across Kansas are connecting with Adam’s message of leading from the middle to lower costs and solve our nation’s biggest problems. Kansans are ready for change.” Newsweek reached out to Marshall's campaign via email on Wednesday for comment. What To Know Sabato’s Crystal Ball said they were initially hesitant to move the race into the Toss-Up category, "but a full-on Republican rescue operation appears underway for Marshall," which helped in part move the needle, the forecaster said. The election forecaster also pointed to the Senate Leadership Fund investing heavily in the race, citing Punchbowl News. "We noted last week that, for the first time all cycle, Republicans now needed to win more Toss-ups than Democrats did in order to win the Senate, and the Kansas move—a GOP-held state—now means Republicans need 4 of the 5 Toss-ups to hold the Senate, while Democrats still just need two," the forecaster said in part. The U.S. Senate races that shifted in the new update, besides Kansas, are Nebraska from Likely Republican to Leans Republican, New Hampshire from Leans Democratic to Likely Democratic, Minnesota from Likely Democratic to Leans Democratic and Mississippi from Safe Republican to Likely Republican. The Cook Political Report currently has the race rated as a Toss-Up as well, adding to the potentially troubling signs for Republicans surrounding the contest. Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Wednesday, "Moving Kansas from Lean Republican to Toss-up is a real warning for Republicans, not a full red alert. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, so any serious threat there means the national environment is biting harder than expected. Senate Leadership Fund already dropped millions into Marshall’s race. That is the tell." Agranoff continued: "When the party has to spend heavily to hold a seat that should be safe, it pulls resources from other fights. Hamilton is not a household name, and Marshall still has the structural edge. A toss-up rating in a deep red state is what forces campaigns to treat it like a real contest instead of a formality. It is not the race that decides the majority by itself, but it is the kind of race that makes holding the majority harder." In his post earlier this week, Trump praised Marshall, calling him a wonderful person who has been given a "bum rap" for allegedly requesting money owed to him by his patients. Marshall had branded the ad targeting his practice a "lie." Trump also threw jabs at Hamilton, saying that he loves high taxes, open borders and added that he wouldn't want the Democrat to be his pastor. The president accused Hamilton of mishandling allegations involving a church camp counselor whom Trump called a child predator. Hamilton's campaign has previously rejected those attacks and also told the Kansas Reflector in July that "there was no attempt at a cover-up" regarding the investigation into the counselor following reports of abuse beginning in 2005, the outlet says. “I can just say that our aim was to make sure that if we got anything wrong, we wanted to get it right,” Hamilton said to the outlet. Hamilton is pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, the Church of the Resurrection. He founded the Kansas City-area congregation in 1990 at age 25, according to his campaign website. What Recent Polling Shows Recent polling shows Hamilton in the lead by a couple of points or a dead heat. Prediction market site Polymarket shows Marshall ahead with 63 percent versus Hamilton's 38 percent on Wednesday afternoon. A YouGov poll showed Hamilton with 48 percent of the potential vote compared to Marshall's 45 percent. One percent said someone else, 5 percent said undecided and 1 percent said they would not vote. The poll surveyed 2,255 likely voters in Kansas from September 24 to October 4 and had a 3.2 percent margin of error. Graham landed 3.4 percent of the vote, and 2.4 percent were undecided. The poll was conducted from October 9-10, 2026, among 1,200 likely voters and had a margin of error of 2.83 percent. The poll surveyed 1,095 likely voters across the state from September 29 to October 1 and had a margin of error of 2.9 percent. news.title: Josh Turek Is Winning Over Iowa Trump Voters, Poll Finds
news.text: A new poll shows that Democrat Josh Turek is winning over people who voted for President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election in the race to be Iowa's next U.S. senator. The Hawkeye State is among this year's most competitive Senate races, as Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson vie for the open seat left by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Polls continue pointing to a tight race between the two candidates after their first debate last week, where tariffs, immigration and voting records played a major role. Both candidates have also exchanged verbal blows regarding the state's economy and the best path forward as Iowans express concerns about inflation and surging fuel costs. The new poll from YouGov comes after Turek and Hinson faced off in a second debate on Tuesday night. Josh Turek vs. Ashley Hinson: What Latest Polls Show After Debate In the YouGov poll, which surveyed 2,245 likely Iowa voters from October 6 to October 12, Turek led Hinson 47 percent to 46 percent, with 4 percent of voters still undecided. And not only did Turek lead in the most recent poll between the two candidates, it also appears he is winning over Iowans who previously voted for Trump. According to the poll, 41 percent of respondents backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, compared with 52 percent who voted for Trump. Given Turek's current edge, the results suggest he has won support from at least some voters who previously cast ballots for Trump. The margin of error was 3.1 percent. Turek's lead over Hinson is narrower in the YouGov poll than in other recent surveys. A poll by Suffolk University conducted from October 1 to October 4 gave him a 4-point lead over Hinson, 48 percent to 44 percent. Turek had a 2-point lead over Hinson in several other recent polls, including a Beacon Research analysis from September 24 to September 28 that favored him over Hinson at 49 percent to 47 percent. An InsiderAdvantage poll held on September 22 and September 23 gave Turek a 1-point lead over Hinson at 47 percent to 46 percent, whereas a Marist University poll taken from September 17 to September 20 gave Turek a heftier 8-point lead over Hinson, 50 percent to 42 percent. Several polls have also shown Hinson ahead. A recent one by Emerson College on October 5 and October 6 favored Hinson for the race at 47 percent to Turek's 45 percent. A CNN poll conducted from September 29 to October 5 also gave Hinson a 2-point lead, at 45 percent to Turek's 43 percent. Hinson carried the same 2-point leads over Turek in two Quantus Insights polls on September 28 and September 29, and a 1-point lead in a New York Times/Siena University poll taken from September 22 to October 1. Newsweek reached out to the campaigns for Turek and Hinson by email on Wednesday. Since the second debate between the two candidates was held on Tuesday night, it did not influence the outcome of the YouGov poll. The poll also allowed some insight into Trump's approval in Iowa, with the majority disapproving of the president's performance. When asked if they approved of Trump's work as president so far, 29 percent said they strongly approved, while 17 percent said somewhat approved. Five percent said they somewhat disapproved, while 49 percent said they strongly disapproved. One percent said they were unsure. What Prediction Markets Show Prediction markets show a less tight race. Both Polymarket and Kalshi show Hinson with a generous lead over Turek. On Polymarket, Hinson is favored to win the Senate race at 57 percent to Turek's 42 percent. She has a slightly greater lead on Kalshi, where she is favored to win at 58 percent to Turek's 42 percent. Why the Iowa Senate Race Matters in the 2026 Midterms This year's midterm elections could flip control of the House and Senate as Republican candidates work to overcome widespread American concerns tied to the economy, inflation, rising fuel costs and the Iran war. Although Iowa has voted Republican in the Senate elections since 2008, the state has also had a history of voting for presidential candidates from both political parties, making the current political environment a competitive one. Trump won Iowa the last three election cycles, but before that, former President Barack Obama won the state twice. The recent poll delivered encouraging news for Turek's campaign, considering the last time Democrats won an Iowa Senate election was 18 years ago, when incumbent Senator Tom Harkin defeated his Republican opponent, Christopher Reed. In the elections since, Ernst and Republican Chuck Grassley have held control of Iowa's two Senate seats. What Happens Next Early voting in Iowa began Tuesday and will continue through November 2. news.title: AOC, JD Vance Head to Michigan as Polls Show Tight El-Sayed-Rogers Race
news.text: New York Democrat Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Vice President JD Vance will make competing appearances in Michigan on Thursday as they campaign for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Republican rival Mike Rogers, respectively, injecting national political star power and potential 2028 presidential intrigue into one of the country's most closely watched races. Vance is scheduled to headline a Trump 47 Committee rally in Monroe, Michigan, while Ocasio-Cortez will join El-Sayed for events in Iron Mountain and Marquette. In a statement announcing the campaign swing, Ocasio-Cortez said El-Sayed had "built a winning coalition with an agenda to bring down costs for Michigan families" and said she was excited to join him during the final stretch of the race. El-Sayed welcomed the endorsement, calling Ocasio-Cortez a "critical partner" during the primary and saying he looked forward to campaigning with her in the closing weeks. Vance's appearance comes as Republicans seek to shore up support in one of the country's most closely watched Senate races. During an earlier Michigan visit alongside Rogers, Republican National Committee spokesman Hunter Lovell said that "President Trump and Vice President JD Vance are leading the charge to elect a powerhouse Republican ticket in Michigan." Newsweek contacted the campaigns of El-Sayed and Rogers for comment. Why Michigan Matters Michigan, a perennial presidential battleground, is expected to be one of the most competitive Senate battlegrounds in the country, helping determine which party controls the chamber after the midterm. The dueling appearances by Ocasio-Cortez and Vance give Michigan voters a rare chance to compare two of the most prominent younger voices in their respective parties. The events could offer clues about which political messages resonate in a state that has repeatedly played a decisive role in national elections. Democratic strategist Joel Payne told The Hill that Michigan's Senate race could have implications well beyond November. "The one race in 2026 that will impact what happens in 2028 is the Michigan Senate race," he said, adding that the contest "will set the tone for the 2028 primary field." A July Michigan poll found Ocasio-Cortez polling third among prospective 2028 Democratic presidential contenders, behind only former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Senator Jon Ossoff, while finishing ahead of California Governor Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris. More than 20 percent of respondents were undecided. What the Latest El-Sayed-Rogers Polls Show Six polls conducted in late September and early October have given El-Sayed a lead from between 1 and 7 percentage points. The newest, an InsiderAdvantage survey of 1,200 likely voters conducted October 9-10, put El-Sayed at 48 percent and Rogers at 46 percent, with 5 percent undecided. Wedgewood Polls was in the field the two days prior and put El-Sayed at 53 percent to Rogers' 47 percent among 607 likely voters. Other recent surveys showed a race inside the margin of error. Quantus Insights found El-Sayed up 48 percent to 47 percent among 744 likely voters polled October 5-6. YouGov, working with a much larger sample of 3,947 likely voters September 22-October 4, also landed on a one-point gap, 49 percent to 48 percent. news.title: Ninth Circuit SLAPS DOWN Newsom law restricting ICE operations
news.text:
A new California law requiring federal immigration agents to wear identification during their operations was permanently slapped down by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.

Critics of Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations say masked and unidentifiable agents pose a risk to illegal alien targets as well as the greater public.

'No set of circumstances exist under which the Act would be valid.' 

On Wednesday, the three-judge panel of the appeals court said the state could not restrict federal operations without congressional approval.

"We conclude ... the No Vigilantes Act attempts to directly regulate the United States in its performance of governmental functions," Judge Mark J. Bennett wrote. "No set of circumstances exist under which the Act would be valid."

The ruling said the law violated the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution. The U.S. Department of Justice had sued to stop the identification law as well as another restriction barring federal agents from using masks during operations.

In April, the same court struck down a similar restriction issued by California.

"If a state law directly regulates the governmental conduct of the United States without congressional authorization, it is void irrespective of whether the regulated activities are essential to federal functions or operations, and irrespective of the degree to which the state law interferes with such functions or operations," Bennett wrote at the time.

More than a dozen other states have similar laws intended to oppose federal immigration operations.

A request for comment from the governor's office was not returned in time for publication.

First Assistant United States Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli has responded with ridicule to other efforts by Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) to restrict ICE operations.

"If you want to regulate federal agents, you have to win a federal election," Essayli responded to Newsom over new restrictions at the end of September.

"Until then, you have no jurisdiction," Essayli added. "Accordingly, I have advised DHS to disregard your bill attempting to ban safe and effective less-lethal tools that agents need to escalate dangerous situations."

Newsom has tried to position himself as the foremost opponent to the president's policy in an apparent campaign to increase his name recognition and run for president.

In the most recent polling, the governor falls far behind Kamala Harris in the race for the Democratic nomination, with support from only 15% of voters, compared to 30% for Harris.

Newsom has also indicated that he would not run for president if Harris decided to run again after losing to President Donald Trump in 2024.
